The New Informants: Betrayal of Confidentiality in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy by Christopher Bollas and David Sundelson. Published by Karnac Books, London, 1995; 204 pages; £16.95.

Paul Gordan

Paul Gordan

London

Paul Gordan  

Confidentiality is so central to the process of psychotherapy that we take it for granted. There are few psychotherapists, I suspect, who would quarrel with the idea. And yet, no sooner do we subscribe to the principle than we go on to breach it as a matter of course. We speak about our patients in supervision and to colleagues; some contact GPs as a routine practice. We speak about patients in professional meetings. Some people speak about them in more public fora or write about them, albeit in a disguised form. Where is the confidentiality in all this? Let me leave the question there for the moment.

‘Why have psychoanalysis and psychotherapy allowed the destruction of confidentiality between clinician and patient?’ This is the question, starkly put, that psychoanalyst Christopher Bollas and US lawyer David Sundelson set out to answer in this timely, provocative and salutary book. Unlike lawyers, journalists and priests, they argue, psychotherapists have allowed their privileged relationship to be destroyed.

In the United States, the 1976 Tarasoff judgement obliges therapists to give a warning of a patient's violent intentions. Tarasoff was a student at the University of California-Berkeley who was murdered by another student whom she was dating and who was in psychotherapy at the student health service. Tarasoff's parents successfully sued the university for negligence in failing to warn their daughter. So too child abuse reporting statutes which now exist in every one of the 50 states in the USA require a therapist to report to the authorities any physical or sexual abuse alleged, whether it was perpetrated by the patient or by another person.

Bollas and Sundelson take the profession to task for its failure to respond adequately to such developments. In particular, they argue, psychotherapists, psychiatrists and psychologists have singularly failed to explain their position; they have failed to provide the ‘detailed and theoretically coherent account’ of what the laws actually do to the patient-therapist relationship. The analysand and the psychoanalyst have to be completely free to speak and ‘experience the monstrous’ if psychotherapy is to have any meaning. It is precisely this that the Tarasoff ruling and the child abuse reporting statutes prevent. The ‘gruesome paradox’ of the Tarasoff ruling, the authors argue, is that in some respects it may actually prevent the violent - actually, potentially or just in fantasy - from seeking help and may thus ultimately increase levels of violence in certain individuals. ‘The incursion into clinical space of third-party interests now means that the practising psychoanalyst's blank screen is littered with legal strictures that demand various forms of compliance’ (p. 90). Trainees now learn to cooperate actively with laws, regulations and health care inquiries in a culture ‘that has lost its sense that confidentiality is indispensable to the practice of psychotherapy’ (p. 73).

Commentary by a Psychoanalytic Psychotherapist

Joanna Ryan

Joanna Ryan

44 Lordship Road, London N16 0QJ

Joanna Ryan  

The general tenor of this session is one of insufficient empathy on the part of the therapist and an undigested fullness which contributes to a sense of deadness in the written material as presented by the therapist. The style of presentation is at times strikingly impersonal and distancing: for example, descriptions of the patient's feelings are put in the form of ‘the experience was one of …’ rather than ‘her experience …’, and such impersonality occurs several times. This reluctance to enter the patient's world is also seen in the rather wooden and unproductive nature of some of the comments and interpretations offered later. The therapist describes the sessions with her patient as ‘full and interesting’ but I can only agree with the first part of this description. It remains quite unclear what the therapist finds interesting.

The patient is introduced as being ‘a lesbian woman’. We are not told whose description this is - the patient's or the therapist's. If it is the patient's words, we are not told anything about the status this self-description has in her life, or any of the complexities that might be involved in this. The bald description suggests a fixity and a definiteness that may or may not apply. Why, furthermore, is the patient's sexual preference foregrounded in this way, as the opening statement? We are given no clues about this or its possible relevance to the clinical material to follow, and indeed the relevance, if there is any, is not made apparent. We are given no idea what the patient's possible conflicts about her sexuality might be, or how this relates to any therapeutic issues, yet her sexuality is made into a defining attribute of her. The therapist's act in making this opening statement is baffling.

In the next statement we are told that the patient has never had a sexual relationship with a man as a follow-up to the description of her as a lesbian. Again the relevance of this to the clinical material that follows seems to be almost non-existent, and certainly no connections are made by the therapist, so once again we are left wondering what this statement is doing here. Is this an important source of conflict or anxiety for the patient, or is this rather a concern of the therapist's? More important, however, is the implication that this fact is the most noteworthy aspect of the patient's lesbianism, rather than anything that might characterize the patient's actual sexual relationships with women. To describe someone thus is to make her lesbianism into a failure of heterosexuality, into a lack of relationships with men. It suggests a privileging of heterosexuality on the part of the therapist, which is all the more problematic for not being explicitly stated as the viewpoint from which the patient is seen.

Laurie Wright

Laurie Wright

ISA, London

Laurie Wright  

Josephine Klein has here gathered together a collection of essays which discuss the personal development of the skills and reflections which have gone into her therapeutic practice. The essays begin with a brief section on ethical values and considerations in the field of psychotherapy, followed by a second group which offer theoretical and clinical thinking about work with patients. The final part, again very brief, would fit well into a section entitled ‘Questions for further consideration in the field of psychotherapy’. It consists of two disparate papers: one is a critique of the differences between Anglo and American psychoanalytic theory, and the other addresses the professions' thinking about the changing role of fathers in families.

The highlight of the book is an essay entitled ‘Patients not ready for interpretations’. This is a thoughtful paper, addressing very difficult issues about the assessment and referral of more disturbed patients, particularly those often designated ‘unanalysable’. Klein makes a case for taking these patients into work with psychoanalytically oriented therapists, stating:

… There are simply too many disturbed people whom we are not even trying to understand how to help. Some of these are helped by alternative methods, but there are methods and insights that psychoanalytically based practitioners have, which could be useful, if we could make up our minds to learn how to use them. (p. 98)

What struck me is Klein's insistence that clinicians should maintain an open interpretation of assessment criteria when considering patients for therapy, emphasizing the need to step outside rigid diagnostic expectations in order to approach those patients suffering more severe disturbance. Klein outlines a set of factors which she uses when assessing these questionably less-analysable patients, which begins with an attempt to discover whether the person possesses an understanding of what therapists and patients do together. This interested me as being blatantly obvious but a consideration which I have never fully thought through. Nor do I remember it being discussed in my training. It is an important point. Encountering therapy for the first time is an odd experience and, for the uninitiated or for someone with disturbed thought processes, therapy can seem bizarre. Klein's point is that, if an environment is incomprehensible, it will not be conducive to the development of a trusting alliance and will consequently stymie the therapeutic process.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

London

Paul Gordon  

What is it about the work of the neurologist Oliver Sacks that makes him read by thousands of people, people who could not write, any more than I could, 100 meaningful words about the workings of the human brain? There are, it seems, several related answers to this question. Principally, Sacks is a marvellous teller of stories. He has sought to reinstate the great nineteenth-century tradition of clinical narration that his intellectual mentor, the outstanding Soviet psychologist A.R. Luria, spoke of in a remark quoted by Sacks in the preface to his earlier collection, The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat: ‘The power to describe, which was so common to the great nineteenth-century neurologists and psychiatrists, is almost gone now … it must be revived’. That Sacks has revived this is unquestionable. He has a formidable ability to inhabit other worlds and to describe them almost from within. Of course, he never is inside. Inevitably he is always the observer but this does not mean that he is detached. And it is this lack of detachment, I think, that makes him so appealing.

Jessica Evans

Jessica Evans

London

Jessica Evans  

When those in the analytic community make reference to wider cultural forms for purposes of metaphor or of illustration of psychic processes they generally turn to a ‘high cultural’ medium of expression such as art or literature rather than popular culture. Photography is likely to be overlooked as part of a flickering world of superficial appearance and bound up with instrumental and commercial imperatives and ways of thinking. It seems to be an irredeemable aspect of mass culture: ephemeral, banal, insubstantial. But photography is central to the twentieth-century symbolic landscape and firmly integrated into the ways we manage our identities and have them managed for us. There can be few of us who have not attempted to control our image of ourselves by posing for a photograph or tearing up the one that makes us feel uncomfortable. The use of the camera is now essential to the experience of weddings, birthdays, holidays, and other rites of passage. Photography thus operates at the boundaries of the private world of the family and the publicly encoded world of photographic conventions residing in such genres as the amateur snapshot and the high-street studio portrait. In the context of photographic education and cultural theory Jo Spence had since the mid-70s pioneered a polemical dissection of the hallowed distinctions between inner and outer, public and private, personal and political.

Rod Postans

Prophecy Coles

Prophecy Coles

Inner City Centre, February 1996

Prophecy Coles  

On January 4th 1996 Rod Lewis Making-Postans died suddenly. He had had a ruptured aortic aneurysm. Rod was only 46 and no one was prepared for this abrupt end. But paradoxically his precipitate going is a reminder of his powerful presence. Rod had a large personality that was riven with paradox. He could rage against hypocrisy and incompetence and at the same time be gentle and understanding. He was angry and yet compassionate. He was a man of integrity forged out of suffering. In his early life he had known traumatic losses: the death of his sister and some close friends followed by an early marriage that failed. And his father had died unexpectedly of a heart attack at 65. These events left him vulnerable to self-doubt and depression in spite of his undoubted gifts and intelligence. In his mid-twenties he went to Middlesex Polytechnic and gained a first class honours degree in social science, followed by an MSc, with distinction, in applied psychology. For six years he was a lecturer at Middlesex Polytechnic in psychology, philosophy and political philosophy and published several papers, including a paper on bereavement.* But he was most proud of the jokes he published in Viz and Mad magazines. He began his training at the Lincoln Centre in the mid-80s and soon after joined the Inner City Centre. His work at the Inner City Centre exemplified his attitude to all areas of his life; he committed himself to the work in a wholehearted way. He became the Treasurer and kept exemplary statistics on patients and wrote six-monthly reports on the current work; and his skill as a master builder meant that he could be called upon to sort out minor domestic repairs. In 1992 he married Wendy and they became the first married couple to work for the ICC, though this was all too brief.

I had the privilege of knowing his work as a therapist. I supervised his work for three years. And I have had the painful task of informing his patients about his death. They testify, without exception, to their experience of his integrity and commitment to the work, and both men and women have told me of the transformation within their inner worlds that he facilitated. His sudden death is not only a shock to us all but it is a loss to the therapeutic world.

Response: The Dilemma of Validation

John Morton

John Morton

MRC Cognitive Development Unit, 4 Taviton Street, London WC1H 0AH

John Morton  

There is widespread agreement in the scientific community on a number of facts out memory. It is clear that what is stored in the mind concerning events we have experienced is fragmentary, and that reconstructive processes operate at the time of recall. These reconstructive processes serve to fill out the narrative by inserting routine items which had not been stored at the time (such as the addition of milk to coffee in our memory of yesterday's breakfast), but could also incorporate information from the record of another, similar, event or, possibly, from something read or seen or even imagined. Next time we try to recall the event, it will rarely be possible for us to distinguish between elements which were present in the original and those which were imported during the previous recall.

Given these properties of our cognitive system, it is not surprising that there is agreement that it is possible for suggestible patients to be led to believe falsely that they were sexually abused in childhood. The relevant question concerns the conditions under which this could occur. Lindsay and Read (1994) said in a recent comprehensive review:

There is little reason to fear that a few suggestive questions will lead psychotherapy clients to conjure up vivid and compelling illusory memories of childhood sexual abuse. (p. 294)

However, it is agreed that sustained pressure by an authority figure on a susceptible person would be likely to lead to false beliefs. It is also agreed that use of techniques such as hypnosis could lead to confusion as to whether the source of a particular thought was reality or imagination.

The scenario characteristic of the recovered memory debate is that an adult in their thirties or forties, in therapy for some reason (the reasons most commonly mentioned are depression, sexual dysfunction or eating disorder), comes to believe that they had been sexually abused as a child by their father. As an illustration, I will summarize a case which was brought to court in Denver and reported in the Rocky Mountain News of 2 and 3 November 1995. This report was summarized in the FMS Foundation Newsletter of January 1996. The therapist was ordered to pay $120,857 for implanting false memories of incest. The patient, JB, had sought treatment for post-partum depression in 1990. After a year in therapy the depression had deepened. Eventually dim memories, then detailed recollections, of weekly sexual abuse emerged. According to JB, the therapist would get angry when she questioned these memories, saying, ‘Why don't you just accept this? You want to get better don't you?’ At some stage, hypnosis was used. JB subsequently cut off relations with her parents and siblings.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis76, 695, 1995

Analysing Forms of Aliveness and Deadness of the Transference-Countertransference

Thomas H. Ogden

The sense of aliveness and deadness of the transference-countertransference represents a critical dimension of the analytic experience and may be the single most important measure of the moment-to-moment status of the analytic process. In this paper the author presents four clinical discussions that illustrate the importance of analysing the experience of aliveness and deadness in (of) the transference-countertransference. In each vignette particular emphasis is placed on the use of transference interpretation derived from experience in the countertransference to address the defensive and expressive role of the dynamic movement of aliveness and deadness at a given juncture in an analysis. The role played by the experience of aliveness and deadness in the structure of the patient's internal object world and quality of object relatedness is examined.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis76, 663, 1995

Seduction, Persecution, Revelation

Jean Laplanche

The author argues that seduction is not primarily a fantasy but a ‘real’ situation, which lies at the heart of the other two allegedly primal major scenarios: castration and the primal scene. This statement is not to be confused with an event-based realism as, for this to be achieved, a third category of reality must be postulated. This reality, constantly misconstrued by authors as corresponding to material and psychological reality, is that of the message conveyed and, more specifically in the case of analysis, the enigmatic message. To establish his position the author re-examines Freud's presentation of the Schreber case. The sexual other and his intrusion are the essential points of Freud's analysis in the first part of his study. In the second part, however, desexualization (in the name of love) and a return to the ego, as the centre of the whole process, both being evident in the ‘primary’ sentence from which Freud proposes to derive everything: ‘I (a man) love him (a man)’. This leads us to a consideration of Fichte's concept of Bekanntmachung, the ‘announcement’ by the other and to an argument that the message stemming from the other is irreducible to a projection by the subject, within the three domains of primal seduction, paranoia and religious ‘revelation’.

The Healing Son: The Patient-Practitioner Relationship and Therapeutic Responsibility edited by Susan Budd and Ursula Sharma. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 1994; 230 pages; £13.99.

Gillian Hemmings

Gillian Hemmings

Gillian Hemmings  

At the heart of this collection of essays lies Susan Budd's Transference Revisited. It is a lucid and accessible retelling of the story of Dora, a description of the psychoanalyst's use of transference and a delineation of its evolution in practice to the present day. I have already found it to be an invaluable teaching tool as well as a beautifully written psychoanalytic ‘summa’.

In the final section of the paper, Budd looks at the social identity of psychoanalysis. She takes into account the shifting of the concept of the relationship between therapist and patient from the original medical model to one which is closer, more intuitive and more introspective. She also traces psychoanalysis from its historical roots, when it was necessary to describe it in ways which would make it accessible to the medical establishment. The author feels that the balancing act between the respectability of medical legitimization and the preservation of an internal identity is now somewhat less precarious for the psychoanalytic profession. However it seems that the tightrope is still being walked, as has been demonstrated by recent splits amongst psychoanalytic psychotherapists.

The diverse nature of the authors and their very individual approaches to the concept of the ‘healing bond’ provides the strength and unifying philosophy of this book, although its very range requires an agility of mind on the part of the reader. The editors, Susan Budd, a psychoanalyst with a background in sociology, and Ursula Sharma, a social anthropologist and sociologist, have gathered together papers from various professionals including an anthropologist, a general practitioner, a sociology professor specializing in health, a solicitor, an osteopath and naturopath, and a gynaecologist. Representing a wide range of concerns and experience, they ask questions about the nature of therapeutic responsibility in the healer/patient relationship, the possibility of shared professional responsibility, and the influence of institutions and the State on the healing bond.

Cracking up: The Work of Unconscious Experience by Christopher Bollas. Published by Routledge, London, 1995; 256 pages; £14.99.

Helen Robinson

Helen Robinson

London

Helen Robinson  

In his new book, Cracking Up, Christopher Bollas chooses to give a central position to the work, not of unconscious processes as they manifest themselves in consciousness (and, above all, for the psychoanalyst, all that that entails), but rather to the presence and the workings of unconscious processes as valid and validifying expressions of the self. This validity of the unconscious at work is in relation to others, as well as within the self, in the forms of expression constituting imagining, dreaming, playing, phantasising, but without the extension or elaboration derived from analysis and, as it were, without its necessary application.

As his main hypothesis he asserts that the capacity for and the presence of ‘the freely moving work of the unconscious’, something that is potentially in all of us, rests upon the particular coming together of two of the elements that Freud described in his description of the dream process: the ‘psychically intense’ experiences that constitute the dream ‘event’ and the capacity to ‘crack’ these up through free association. Taking these two elements, Bollas suggests that as human beings we are able to find differing levels of what he calls ‘unconscious freedom’ through ‘the necessary opposition between the part of us that finds truth by uniting disparate ideas (i.e. “condensation”) and the part of us that finds the truth in breaking up those unities’.

Thus, the hypothesis upon which he focuses this new study or set of essays is the capacity of the mind to bring together freely and to take apart freely in a continuum and in a continuing process, a curative and enriching feature in all minds, though not all minds are able to deploy it. Bollas goes on to give variations upon, discourses upon, elaborations upon this central tenet, taken originally from Freud and the riches of the unconscious in the act of dreaming. This text, then, is about the process of unconsciousness per se, as defined in this way, (‘coming together/breaking apart’) and how Bollas sees us as engaging in this. It seemed to me that the riches of such a process of mind, as well as the deprivations for those whose minds are restricted in such coming together and taking apart, are well documented here by reference to those who are able to make such creative use of their unconscious, perhaps in the course of their analysis (but not exclusively so) and those who are restricted, for example by traumata, and whose use of their unconscious is wholly uncreative and sterile. There is reference to the destructive manipulation of unconsciousness in a chapter on the serial killer and a powerful representation of the kind of functioning deployed here to facilitate murderousness freely. An interesting hypothesis about the derivation of such capacities is put forward by Bollas.

Psychoanalytic and Scientific Reasoning

Jim Hopkins

Jim Hopkins

London WC2R 2LS. e-mail: j.hopkins@kcl.ac.uk

Jim Hopkins  

In daily life we find meaning and motive in the actions of persons (and other animals) naturally, spontaneously and continually. Let us speak of the mental capacities, modes of inference, or ways of thinking by which we do so as those of interpretation as Freud did in speaking of the interpretation of dreams. We apply our ability to interpret, in this sense, both to passing events or episodes in behaviour, such as motivated actions and the production of meaningful sentences, and also to lasting results of such behaviour, such as written texts.

Freud intended psychoanalysis to be an interpretive science. To many the idea that something is a matter of interpretation already implies that it cannot be scientific or even objective, so that this idea seems paradoxical. Such a dismissal, however, ignores the fundamental role which interpretation plays in our lives and understanding generally. Our interactions with others are mediated by interpretation of their behaviour, and our fate often depends upon how we do this: for example, on our capacity to detect and respond to love or hate, friendship or emnity, and many other motives. Again, it is through interpretation, taken broadly, that we understand language; and much of what we know seems registered in language or understood through our use of it. We cannot generally claim a firmer grasp on any of the phenomena we use language to describe than we can on the language which we use to describe them; and to use language with grasp is to use it according to determinable rules, and hence in a way which can be interpreted. This indicates that there is a sense in which we understand nothing better than our own language, and in that sense, ourselves. In this perspective interpretation could be regarded as prior to science; and the limits of interpretation - whatever they are - would be those of communicable science as well.1

It seems right to say that the pervasive role of interpretation in psychoanalysis sets it apart from many other disciplines and from those which we regard as paradigms of science. As the above indicates, however, this does not entail that psychoanalytic hypotheses lack objectivity or empirical support, which is often the issue in disputes as to whether psychoanalysis is to be regarded as scientific2. In what follows I sketch a comparison between interpretive with scientific thinking, which also indicates how psychoanalytic conclusions might be regarded as well founded.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Psychoanalysis and the psychotherapies based on it have proliferated without the benefit of scientific validation for 100 years, growing into a world-wide movement of tremendous cultural significance. Yet, we constantly face the embarrassment of not having a body of research firmly demonstrating its scientific basis. When Eysenck threw down the gauntlet in 1953, declaring that there was no scientific evidence for the value of the psychotherapies, that they were no more effective than ‘spontaneous remission’ in control groups and calling for the end of psychotherapy training, he did us a favour by stimulating research studies. Over the next 30 years, outcome trials and statistical wars took place. By the 1980s it was agreed by researchers that psychotherapy did not just exist in the eye of the beholder: it was an actual phenomenon. The psychological treatments as a whole were found to have a ‘modestly positive effect’ compared with no treatment, but research was unable to distinguish between types of therapy at outcome: in the words of the Dodo in a widely-read research review, ‘Everybody has won and all must have prizes’ (Luborsky et al. 1975), as all types of therapy were found to be equally effective using the crude research tools available. More sophisticated process research is needed but, in order to look at the processes distinctive to analytic work, it would be necessary to intrude into the sessions by tape or video recordings to gather evidence, which is looked upon with horror by clinicians in Britain because of the confidential and intimate nature of the treatment.

So how do we solve this dilemma? Do we struggle on attempting to find acceptable scientific evidence for psychoanalytic principles, or do we look at science itself and argue that it is changing, evolving new scientific models that could make valid inquiry into intersubjectivity and the interpersonal human ecology possible? In March 1996 the BJP third joint conference with the Freud Museum took place, which brought together five distinguished speakers who have been thinking and working in the area of the scientific status of psychoanalysis. We present their papers in this issue, beginning with Joseph Schwartz, previously a physicist, who looks at the scientific status of science itself. Then we have papers by David Smith and Karl Figlio that discuss problems of applying the scientific method to clinical realities, followed by a paper by the philosopher James Hopkins from King's College, London, who strikingly demonstrates by using the analytical tools of philosophy that, when carefully examined, psychoanalytic reasoning and scientific reasoning employ exactly the same rules of inference. The final conference paper is by Peter Fonagy, professor of psychoanalysis at University College London, whose paper spoke of the changing influence of psychoanalytic thought as indicated by the decline in citations in learned journals. Prof. Fonagy points a way forward for research without which child analysis is imperilled. The conference was chaired by Dr Michael Conran, who offers his chairman's comments.

Laurie Wright  

In this paper I will be looking at the nature of the transference relationship, and asking whether it can be seen as a template for understanding other relationships outside the analytical setting. I will be positing the idea that there are relationships with profound similarities to the analytic relationship in areas as diverse as the creative arts and family generations. It is my feeling that through a close inspection of creative transference relationships, such as the relationship between a reader and a text, we can begin to understand how dyadic transference relations are formed and acted out. I am also hoping to show that through other transference relationships we can learn to interpret and analyse the feelings of countertransference. I am suggesting that transference and countertransference feelings are not restricted to the analytical setting.

A Core Phantasy in Violence

Rosine Jozef Perelberg

In this paper the author develops the hypothesis that for some patients there is a core phantasy in their violence that is related to their beliefs about their own procreation. Drawing on her experience of trying to understand and treat psychoanalytically one such patient, the author illustrates how it may be possible to apprehend that there is a pattern in which violence is exercised, a plot or narrative that allows the underlying phantasies to be identified. The violent act tells a story, which is a personal myth of creation and contains both pre-oedipal and distorted oedipal theories. These ideas are then discussed in the context of Freud's writings on violence (Heftigkeit) as well as in relation to a second particularly violent patient.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis76, 1083, 1995

The Infantile in the Analytic Relationship

Florence Guignard

The author examines the narcissistic and relational aspects of the preconscious functioning of the analytic couple in order to bring out the drive-related, developmental and structural elements of the infantile in their relationship. She considers that any disruption of the specific tone of an analysis indicates a change in the level of drive excitation, which is experienced unconsciously in the transference and countertransference as the loss of a significant internal object and gives rise to a representational deficiency. Where this is due to the impact of the infantile-in-the-patient on his own preconscious, the analyst suffers a blind spot. As long as he can desist from using ‘blocking representations’, the effect will be to repress the unrepresented wish and at the same time to create a framing and containing preform beneficial to the treatment. In the author's view, the analyst deals with his blind spot by a ‘work of the negative’ a la Andre Green, through denial of his fantasy of seduction by the infantile omnipotence of the analysand. This model can also be used to investigate the termination criteria of the analyst's own analysis and the economic situation of repression in the psychoanalyst's work.

Psychotherapy and Memory - An Attachment Perspective

Jeremy Holmes MD MRCP

Jeremy Holmes

Barnstaple, Devon EX31 4JB

Jeremy Holmes  

Early Freudian concepts of memory are contrasted with those of contemporary psychoanalysis. Freud and Breuer's project to ‘remove the amnesias’ has been replaced with a more subtle, context-bound view of memory, in which it is not only facts but their associated affects that need to be retrieved. The attachment-based typology of insecure attachment patterns provides a framework for thinking about memories in psychotherapy, which may be suppressed, overwhelming or unintegrated. Memories are constructions and are therefore inherently unreliable. ‘Normal’ and traumatic memories are processed, stored and retrieved in different ways. The controversy over recovered memories and the false memory syndrome are reviewed in the light of this argument. Therapeutic implications are discussed.

What is Science? What is Psychoanalysis? What is to Be Done?

Joseph Schwartz PHD

Joseph Schwartz

2 Lancaster Drive, London NW3 4HA

Joseph Schwartz  

Introduction

I want to thank the Freud Museum and the British Journal of Psychotherapy for putting together such a timely conference. Recent attacks on psychoanalysis and psychotherapy have invariably raised the question of the scientific credibility of psychoanalysis, a charge that is so clouded over by an ignorance of science that it hs been difficult to formulate an adequate response. I have been particularly struck by the spectacle of novelists like Fay Weldon and literary critics like Frederick Crews confidently accusing psychoanalysis of being unscientific without their giving any evidence that they know anything at all about science.

Nevertheless the charge seems to stick. We all seem to believe at some level that psychoanalysis may not be scientific in the usual way but …. Following the ‘but’ are a number of responses: but psychoanalysis is valid in its own right; but psychoanalysis is trying to become more scientific by doing controlled studies; but psychoanalysis is an hermeneutic art and not a science at all and it is just not fair to judge it by the strict standards of science.

All these responses accept uncritically a notion of a science that is objective, precise and, above all, certain. Such a science is a mythic science, not a real science, a myth that originated with the formation of the Royal Society in 1660 following the Restoration and that became consolidated in the late 19th century with the public relations activities of the Movement for the Endowment of Research in Britain and the American Association for the Advancement of Science in the United States.

There is a dual aspect of science, long known to working scientists. There is a set of actual practices and bodies of knowledge that bring us into more intimate engagement with the natural world. And there is a set of social representations of science, an ideology of science, which in these debates is frequently called a positivist view of science. When Fay Weldon calls psychoanalysis unscientific she calls upon the ideology of science in an attempt to discredit psychoanalysis. She knows and we know that it is a very bad thing to be unscientific. How can we trust something that is unscientific?

The therapist writes about a 16-year-old adolescent boy who has been in twice-weekly psychotherapy for a year. We are told that Paul presented with somatic symptoms: headaches and high blood pressure, for which no organic cause was found. These are relatively unusual psychosomatic symptoms in an adolescent, and suggest the possibility of early problems in affect regulation and the psychic representation of primitive affects. This links with what we are told about Paul's long-standing problems in controlling his aggression and rage; he is described as having very little internal control. He has also used drugs and alcohol to deal with unbearable affects. Though we know little about his infancy and early childhood, and so have little knowledge of his developmental history, the theme of expulsion, being pushed out too soon, a fundamental lack of a sense of containment, seems to be important in making sense of Paul's experience. I gained the impression that there was a lot of anxiety, overt and unacknowledged, in the family, due partly to the older sister's severe mental illness, and possibly the effects of father's immigration experience.

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Letchworth

Phil Mollon  

Hedges has something important to say about some of the patients who cause us most anguish and anxiety. He is writing about a fundamental level of disturbance which results from a failure to establish bonding and connectedness with the primary

556

caregiver. The basic idea is that if the infant cannot ‘organize’ meaningfully around the attuned presence of the mother, then he/she resorts to attempts to organize around aspects of self, its own body, or inanimate objects. Although the wish to seek connection and to bond is still present, contact is now dreaded, threatening a repetition of the original trauma of misattunement. The transference resulting from this level of disturbance is psychotic, primitive, intense and extremely difficult to manage. Much of the analytic speaker's (Hedges's term for the ‘patient’) energies are directed towards avoiding real emotional contact. As contact is eventually established, the analytic listener is perceived as malevolent - as the ‘psychotic mother’.

Hedges draws upon some of the exciting analytic work that has developed in the last twenty years. He owes a particular debt to Kohut who, in the American context, did much to establish the importance of the analytic relationship in the healing process. Kohut observed that when the patient experiences the analyst as empathically attuned, he/she has a sense of well-being; when the analyst is experienced as not attuned, certain patients become temporarily (reversibly) psychotic, hypochondriacal, thoughtdisordered or paranoid. However, Kohut considered that, whilst patients with narcissistic disturbance could benefit from the analytic process, those with schizoid problems were beyond analytic help because the danger of uncontrolled and irreversible regression to psychosis was too great. Hedges, by contrast, believes it is possible to help these people to enter and work through the ‘organizing experience’ in relation to the therapist. In discussing this level of analytic work he also draws upon the similar ideas of other theorists: for example, Tustin and Grotstein have both written of ‘black hole’ anxiety; Winnicott wrote of ‘unthinkable agonies’; Balint spoke of the ‘basic fault’; Mahler described ‘annihilation anxiety’. Hedges does not consider the Kleinian concept of persecutory anxiety, but he views the organizing experience as developmentally prior to the onset of object relational splitting and projection (a view rather similar to that of Tustin).

Chairman's Comments: Psychoanalysis - A Disreputable Profession?

Michael Conran MD

Michael Conran

29 Hamilton Gardens, St John's Wood, London NW8 9PU

Michael Conran  

The experimental method is concerned only with the search for objective truths, not with any search for subjective truths … The greatest truths, indeed, are at bottom simply a feeling in our mind; that is what Descartes meant by his famous aphorism.

Art is I; Science is We.

(Claude Bernard 1865)

The word Science in the title of this conference appears in single inverted commas. We are at once alerted to an ambiguity about this word which the conference organizers seem to share. To be sure the word science strictly means knowledge, no more, no less. However that may be, everyone knows it is bandied about as an euphemism for much else. Science is an activity pursued by people called scientists. It is a professional and social group which, at any given time in modern history, determines the credentials of acceptance into the scientific establishment. In the last half century, certainly within medicine, it has come to mean measurement. Here and there it is not distinguished from technology. For some it is tantamount to a religion, or an anti-religion. It is worshipped, feared, adored and loathed. It is the venue of curiosity, investigation, wonderment and beauty. To others it is the embodiment of ugliness and destruction.

These then are some of the attributes of science as they are of knowledge and, perhaps more to the point, of thought itself. For we know that thinking is hard work, and it is painful. Many would sooner die than think, and sometimes they do just that.

Freud (1927) is similarly ambiguous. In one breath he speaks of ‘our science’ (psychoanalysis). In the same essay he restricts ‘scientific work’ for our knowledge of external reality. Inner, or psychic, reality is, and then again is not, accessible to scientific enquiry. Or so it seems. It is a muddled area.

For the purposes of this conference science predominantly means a scientific community into which psychoanalysis and psychoanalysts are or are not acceptable. And if they are not acceptable, what is to be done about it?

John Rowan  

This book is by a psychoanalyst who has also been involved with group work (especially Bion), as well as marital and family work. He has written several books, papers and chapters on brief psychotherapy before and runs the Brief Psychotherapy Clinic at Wisconsin University where he is a professor. He evidently developed a late interest in Jung.

It is written in an extremely dogmatic style, and the author throws around epithets like ‘malignant’ and ‘benign’ as if they were legal tender. He uses labels like ‘paranoid’ and ‘borderline’ with great freedom as if there were no questions about their application. He regards some patients as being impossible, and fails to entertain the possibility that they are only impossible within the confines of a rigid system of treatment.

Often there is an incredible oversimplification, such as when the author quotes with approval Beels's comment that schizophrenia was a housing problem. ‘By this he meant that schizophrenics did best in small boarding-houses where they could keep their distance, such as from dinner table conversation, yet there was always somebody up to have some slight company’ (p. 18). This seems to me a custodial approach which has little to do with psychotherapy.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis77, 217, 1996

Playing with Reality: I. Theory of Mind and the Normal Development of Psychic Reality

Peter Fonagy and Mary Target

The authors of this paper discuss changes in the child's perception of psychic reality during normal development, highlighting a major shift in the child's understanding of minds (‘theory of mind’) at the oedipal stage. They illustrate this transition with material from the analysis of a 4-year-old girl. They maintain that the very young child uses two forms of psychic reality, which they have called ‘psychic equivalent’ and ‘pretend’ modes, which differ primarily in the assumed relationship between internal and external realities. The integration of the dual modes into a singular reflective mode is normally completed by about the age of 4, with affect leading cognition: the child first understands that people have different feelings, then that they may have different thoughts about the same external reality. The authors describe normal psychological growth and neurotic pathology, in which the integration of these two modes of functioning has been only partly achieved.



Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy10(2): 143-54, 1996

Bearing the Unbearable - Working with the Abused Mind

Roger Kennedy

The paper discusses some issues concerned with the psychoanalytic treatment of adults who have memories of being sexually abused as children. Issues covered include the nature of the abused mind, the nature of memories of abuse and the way that the abusing experience may be repeated in the analysis by making an emotional impact of a particular kind on the analyst. The title refers to how the analyst may need to help the patient bear unbearable experiences which the immature abused child could not deal with effectively. Clinical material from an adult analysis is presented to highlight the latter theme. But, in addition, the author's extensive experience of working with severely broken-down families, who are admitted as inpatients to the Family Unit of the Cassel Hospital, London, is also drawn on in order to clarify some of the difficult issues that arise from working with the abused patient.

Clinical Practice and the Architecture of the Mind by Robert Langs. Published by Karnac, London, 1995; 149 pages; £15.95.

Adrian Dickinson

Adrian Dickinson

London

Adrian Dickinson  

In this book Robert Langs explains and examines the implications of the theories he has developed through his communicative and empowered psychotherapies. Although he is often seen as a maverick figure, his ideas, particularly those of the metaphoric or narrative communication between patient and therapist being direct rather than transferential from earlier figures or from internal fantasy, have had considerable influence (Casement 1985). Here, distinguishing between the conscious and the ‘deep unconscious system’, he argues that the latter system of the ‘emotionprocessing mind’ has a wisdom and a directness lacking in the conscious system.

Langs argues that as well as the ‘superficial’ (or Freudian) unconscious in which the normal modes of unconscious functioning can be observed through symptoms, behaviour and language there is an autonomous ‘deep unconscious system’, the effects of which can be observed and analysed in the ‘unique situation’ of personal therapy. This deep unconscious system, in a way that I find not that far removed from Freud's concept of manifest and latent dream content, communicates through narratives that, when ‘decoded’, reveal the patient's unconscious anxieties and wishes about the preservation of the ‘secure frame’ of the analytic session, together with observation of its ‘ground rules’. All this will be familiar to readers of his earlier books.

What is interesting in this book is his clear exposition of his communicative approach to psychotherapy (through fictional clinical vignettes designed to illustrate his practice), and his speculation about the evolutionary advantages of a dual system of mental ‘emotion processing’ in which the conscious system is totally separate from the ‘deep unconscious’. But despite the convincing nature of his vignettes I am left with a sense of thinness. Why? Partly it derives from the language. Langs's idiolect is mechanistic and behaviouristic - emotions are to be ‘processed’, ‘triggers’ to be ‘decoded’ - and the ‘deep unconscious’ he discovers seems to be a stimulus/response system designed to maintain the psychic status quo.

Abiding Values and the Creative Present: Psychoanalysis in the Spectrum of the Sciences

David Black

David Black

30 Cholmley Gardens, London NW6 1AG

David Black  

If psychoanalysis is a science, then it differs in important ways from other sciences, such as physics, which are often taken as paradigmatic in the field. It does so above all because living beings place a demand upon time. Out of this demand value springs. In the case of human beings, this demand, studied in its greatest depth by psychoanalysis, is not only for the values of survival and reproductive success but also for the values that conduce to psychological growth and health. To incorporate this objective importance of values into a scientific picture involves a huge shift in the way in which we conceive the world, with implications for the wider perception of the sciences in general.

An Attachment-Based Approach to Working with Clients Affected by HIV and AIDS

Chris Purnell

Chris Purnell

Shrewsbury SY3 8HS

Chris Purnell  

This paper examines the relevance of attachment theory in the provision of psychological support to people who are affected by HIV. It highlights the themes of change, loss and vulnerability as central to the issues which confront members of this client group. Indications are provided of a range of attachment-related behavioural responses which can be activated by these conditions, and illustrations are provided of how the activation of attachment behaviour can destabilize the relationships of some clients who are anxiously attached. The concept of a secure base, a term first coined by Mary Ainsworth and developed as a theme by the originator of attachment theory, John Bowlby, is presented as being a central provision by the therapist in work with clients who are affected by HIV, and illustrations are given of how the therapist might begin to help build a secure base for clients who have anxious, internal working models of attachment. The paper concludes with an indication of how an attachment-based approach might be used in working with clients in the terminal stages of HIV-related illness.

Changes in Health Service Utilization by Patients with Severe Personality Disorders before and after Inpatient Psychosocial Treatment

Marco Chiesa MD , Eduardo Lacoponi PHD and Mark Morris MB

Mark Morris

Surrey TW10 7JF

Mark Morris  

Patients with chronic and severe personality disorders place heavy demands on Health and Social Services. In this paper we present the findings of a research study which evaluated the impact of specialized inpatient psychosocial treatment on patterns of Health Service utilization in patients referred for admission to the Cassel Hospital. The comparison between a pre-treatment and a post-treatment sample showed a significant decrease in the use of medical, surgical and psychiatric services in the year following discharge from the hospital. We also found that the post-treatment group relied less on the use of psychotropic medication, on cigarette and alcohol consumption, while the employment rate was increased. This paper adds to the already substantial scientific literature to show that psychotherapy and psychosocial forms of treatment make economic sense, as well as improving the psychological health of patients.

Open to All Possibilities

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

8 St Saviour's Terrace, Larkhall, Bath, Avon BA1 6RL

Fiona Gardner  

I told her I was not in a position to know, but I was open to all possibilities. We would continue to explore.

(Raphling 1994, p. 70)

Some patients now suspect during their psychotherapy that they might have been sexually abused as children (cf. Maguire 1995). The contemporary controversy over the validity of recovered memory while the patient is in treatment calls into question clinical and ethical issues, and so demands some thoughts on clarification and validation of psychoanalytic psychotherapeutic methods, and the significance of reconstruction and construction. This paper, based on clinical work with two patients, is a contribution to the discussion on assessment of emerging memories of abuse and some of the differing aspects of verification. In this article I use the word ‘true’ in the sense of ‘genuine’, and also use the concepts ‘psychic truth’ and ‘psychic reality’ interchangeably to refer to what happens within and between patient and therapist.

Publicity by the False Memory Society may lead therapists, attracted by scientism, to strive for the objective, definable and real. Yet it becomes quickly apparent that positivistic notions of validation have little relevance to the analytic encounter which is characterized and permeated by subjectivity and uncertainty. The practice of psychoanalytic psychotherapy is one where knowledge is seen in constant, dynamic evolution and transformation, and where the link between theory and practice demands elastic and flexible concepts (de Azevedo 1994). The encounter with the patient is primarily intersubjective, and so the shared therapeutic experience is the situation where analytic knowledge emerges through the transference, where reconstructions and constructions are formulated and where interpretations are validated.

Verifiable documentation of childhood sexual abuse, for example through hospital or social services records, is usually not available, and so the assessment and validation of the recovered memories take place in the consulting-room between patient and therapist. There are different levels of investigation in the assessment of emerging memories, with both the manifest and latent, the conscious and unconscious being considered. At the same time as listening to the patient's material there is an awareness of one's own thoughts and feelings. Both patient's and therapist's transferences, associations and formulations are noted alongside body states, as well as the patient's responses to interpretations. It is the psychic reality of both patient and therapist that is then being considered, though there is both a connection and a distinction between the inner experience and the actuality.

Postscript

Sandra Bloom

Sandra Bloom

Sandra Bloom  

In the second part of the paper by van der Kolk and Fisler, which is not reproduced here, the authors studied 36 women and 10 men who met the diagnostic criteria for PTSD in order to record whether, and how, memories of traumatic experiences are retrieved differently from memories of significant but non-traumatic experiences. Thirty-six of the individuals had their most significant traumatic experience in childhood, the remainder as adults, and 75% of the subjects with childhood trauma had external confirmation of the traumatic experience.

All subjects, regardless of age at which the trauma occurred, reported that their initial memory was not in the form of a narrative, but was instead a somatosensory or emotional flashback experience. The study supported the frequently observed difference in the very nature of traumatic vs. normal memory. The essence of traumatic memory is that initially it is not symbolized, but stored as fragmented sensory input related to the traumatic event. Over time, most trauma victims construct a narrative for these sensory imprints. Like all narrative memories, the verbal accounts for what has happened are subject to distortion. However, a large body of research has shown that memories of emotionally highly significant events are subject to less distortion than are memories of everyday experience. There were interesting trends noted between the adult onset trauma group and the childhood onset group as well, trends that are very consistent with clinical experience. The childhood trauma group had significantly more pathological self-soothing behaviors than the adult group, including self-mutilation and bingeing. This supports the notion, which has a growing empirical basis, that childhood trauma gives rise to more pervasive biological dysregulation.

Van der Kolk and Fisler conclude their paper with a reference to their brain imaging study that showed that traumatic memories ‘happen’ principally in the emotional areas of the right hemisphere, and are accompanied by an increase in activity in the visual areas of the brain, signifying that people with PTSD actually ‘see’ their flashbacks, while there is a decrease in the area of the brain in charge of the translation of emotional states into language. This brain imaging study suggests that the notion of ‘speechless terror’ which is part of the trauma response is not merely a popular metaphor, but an experience that is based on altered brain function at the moment of the trauma.

Ian Parker

Ian Parker

Deane Road, Bolton BL3 5AB

Ian Parker  

This paper explores the ways in which psychoanalytic conceptions of self and personal change suffuse culture and so frame the activities of psychotherapists. It is argued that the modern culture which gave issue to psychoanalysis has mutated in recent years into what some writers have termed ‘postmodernity’, and that psychoanalytic notions have also changed. The conceptual device of the ‘discursive complex’ is used to trace how themes of ‘intellectualization’, ‘transference’ and ‘trauma’ which organize modern therapeutic discourse have been augmented, through the development of new forms of communication technology, by postmodern themes of ‘the Symbolic’, ‘Che Vuoi’ and ‘enigmatic signifiers’.

Science does not rest upon solid bedrock. The bold structure of its theories rises, as it were, above a swamp. It is like a building erected on piles. The paper explores the absence of a parental couple in Western culture and psyche and its substitution by masculine omnipotence. The inability of the Western psyche to work through the Oedipus complex is seen as the root of this. This inability is linked to the lack of a gradual working through of ambivalence, and to the reliance, instead, on a massive repression of the attachment to mother and on the conversion of the aggression towards father into the superego. In the novella The Captain's Doll, D.H. Lawrence represents an individuation process in which the male protagonist evolves from a state of extreme infantile bondage into an adult relationship, safeguarding his autonomy. responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Introduction

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

When Freud proposed, in The Interpretation of Dreams, that psychic reality was ‘a particular form of existence not to be confused with material reality’, he made a distinction which proved fundamental in the development of psychoanalysis as a body of knowledge. It implied an independence of spheres: psychic reality did not depend on material reality for its existence. Later in time but no less significant was the identification of the therapist's counter-transference as object of study, source of data (broadly conceived) and link with the patient's affective state.

But what is then validated in the clinical setting? How does psychic reality mesh with psychic truth, and how does psychic truth mesh with historical truth? What if they do not? Does it matter? Does the way that it matters change over time? And if so, where does the pressure for new conceptualizations come from? It could be said that clinicians are always presented with dilemmas about the ‘believability’ of patients' narratives; but that the question has rarely been posed with such fierce difficulty - for everyone concerned - as in the controversy of the last few years over ‘false’ (now ‘recovered’) memories of sexual abuse.

Our authors have the benefit of being able to reflect on this phenomenon after the first wave of social unease has died down (cf. also Mollon, this issue, pp. 397-9; Sinason, ed., forthcoming). The Journal thought it important to promote a dialogue between different perspectives, with their different vocabularies. In this way, perhaps, the essential features of a view may be more keenly perceived. To this end Fiona Gardner explores ‘psychic reality’ within the clinical framework as a force which may create doubt in the mind or acquire its own validity, and thinks through the conditions of that doubt. We reproduce part of a recent North American study by Bessel van der Kolk and Rita Fisler, which surveys the experience of traumatic amnesia as well as the literature on it; it is contextualized by Sandra Bloom, who is familiar with the debate on both sides of the Atlantic. There follows a methodological engagement with the two articles, in which John Morton probes the nature of memory from his starting point as a cognitive psychologist.

Dissociation and the Fragmentary Nature of Traumatic Memories: Introduction

Sandra Bloom

Sandra Bloom

Sandra Bloom  

In America, major social issues tend to get played out in the courts, which is no guarantee of scientific integrity or truth. The ‘false memory syndrome’ originates in the story of one family tragedy that has become a symbol for deep divisions in the social fabric (Fried 1994).

‘False memory syndrome’; ‘recovered memory therapy’; ‘implantation of false memories’; by now, any American who reads the newspapers, reads the weekly news magazines, or watches television has heard these seemingly credible and scientificsounding words. Therapists of all persuasions are routinely told by friends, relatives and even colleagues that they understand how easy it is for therapists to implant false memories of abuse (always referring only to sexual abuse) in the minds of their unwary and disturbed patients. Lawsuits against therapists for practising ‘recovered memory therapy’ are proliferating. Some therapists are being picketed, their patients harassed, the privacy of their homes invaded (Doehr 1994). Attempts are being made in several states to introduce legislation that would disallow any therapy that had not been proven ‘safe and effective’ by the standards similar to those used to test new drugs and that would allow a patient's relatives, even against the wishes of the patient, to sue the therapist for malpractice (Quirk & DePrince 1995).

Sadly, there are several important things missing from this picture. One is that there is as yet no peer-reviewed, published study that supports the view that ‘false memory syndrome’ exists. Another is that there is no apparent way to distinguish between ‘recovered memory therapy’ and any other form of therapy that includes taking a good history from a patient. Another is that there is no scientifically validated evidence to support the proposition that it is possible to implant entire memories of traumatic events into anyone's mind. And finally, there has yet to be a balanced presentation about the vast body of theoretical and research data, deriving from several different disciplines and spanning over 100 years of clinical experience that indicates the significant differences between normal memory, normal forgetting, traumatic memory, and the intrusive re-experiencing of traumatic events. The fact that there has not been such a balanced presentation to the public - despite the obvious and overwhelming amount of data that contradicts most of what the false memory advocates offer as evidence - is what has convinced many in America that this is more of a political and social than scientific debate. Indeed, much of this debate has been conducted in the media, with a one-sided, distorted and sensationalist bias, rather than in professional journals.

Response to Joseph Schwartz

Robert Langs MD and Anthony Badalamenti

Anthony Badalamenti

133 West 72nd Street, Suite 304, New York, NY 10023, USA

Anthony Badalamenti  

Once more, reluctantly, we respond to a discussion of our 1994 paper. In principle, and with considerable support from the literature in both mathematics and physics, we are convinced that the claims made by Dr Schwartz - that our methods, mathematical models and lines of thought are in error - are entirely unfounded. In this connection, we regret that Dr Schwartz did not take the trouble to read the many relevant original papers that specify our methods and their rationales - papers that were accepted by prestigious journals whose knowledgeable editors, trained in both physics and mathematics, had no quarrel with our methodology and the implications we drew from our results (for example, Badalamenti & Langs 1992a, 1992b; Langs & Badalamenti 1990). Had he done so, he might have better understood our approach and the ideas it generated.

At the request of the editor of this Journal, we will respond to the specific arguments made by Schwartz in broad terms. The Poisson Process we unearthed for our speaker duration series clearly calls for a thesis of tension build-up in humans with intentionality. This is an idea that makes commonsense in that the longer a person is silent, the greater the likelihood that he or she will soon speak - a tendency we were able to characterize individually for each subject we studied using specific mathematical models.

We stand by our claim to have measured the work done on the information particle whose values we traced, and we want to point out that the laws of physics hold for all natural processes. These laws are applicable to modern-day information theory and to studies of complex systems - including a wide range of biological phenomena. Further, our evidence for a communicative force field is comparable to what is accepted in physics, and the application of both mechanics and thermodynamics to our data is in keeping similar applications to one-particle systems and is supported by the link between work capacity and entropy - a relationship that we found in our data. And finally, models from physics have frequently been used to clarify and advance the understanding of biological phenomena, for example, membrane transport equations, brain imaging, optics, lung competence and much more.

Commentary by a Child Psychotherapist

Denis Flynn

Denis Flynn

57 Lock Road, Ham, Richmond TW10 7LL

Denis Flynn  

The therapist's account of her work with Paul, aged 16, includes her synoptic view of the problems and background and detailed notes from three sessions. This gives us privileged access not just to this adolescent boy's way of relating, but to some of the feelings evoked in the therapist, her countertransference. My clinical commentary looks at both these things so that, by viewing the psychoanalytic process in detail, we can learn about Paul's internal world and his very troubled relation to his environment.

As I read the background I found myself asking in places whose account of the history is it? Whose belief is it also that Paul will end up like his sister who has suffered a severe manic depressive illness, his or his parents'? I thought initially that Paul's own fears and phantasies are not easily distinguishable from those of others. This may simply be because this is a brief summary and not that Paul takes on the views of others, or vice versa. I shall return to this issue later. Other questions arose for me too. Paul is the youngest by 10 years, so was he a baby or small child when his sister's illness affected her, and did his sister's illness deeply affect his mother and the family? He now has a breakdown in adolescence and, like her, comes to the same clinic. Does all this affect not just him, but his mother, to whom he is very close, and the whole environment for his adolescent transition? Is a severe state of flux observable between his perceptions of internal and external reality, now in adolescence as in early infancy? Lastly, what of any effective paternal elements? For, from what little we heard, I thought the father whom he treats with contempt as a tyrant may have become a figure in his internal world and in his gang-like tendencies in social relationships. As a preliminary historical hypothesis I was asking, ‘Did he observe his mother's fragile state as a baby and equate destructiveness with his own aggression and expressed neediness?’

In therapy we learn how his sense of self has changed for, instead of seeing himself as confused and stupid, he has a more street-wise attitude. But the sophisticated exterior can disappear into incoherence, and he is a mixed-up learner (dyslexia)

Phil Mollon  

As the Scharffs comment in the concluding paragraph to their book, ‘100 years ago, patients whose impairment was due to sexual trauma were the inspiration for Freud's invention of psychoanalysis’ but, as his interests changed, the field moved from the study of trauma and dissociation to intrapsychic conflict, neurosis and repression. As a result, ‘in this long interval we did not advance our knowledge about actually traumatized patients and consequently had less to offer them than we might have’. Surely so! Indeed much of the recent understanding of the long-term consequences of childhood trauma has developed outside the main psychoanalytic traditions, having been inspired partly by the appreciation of post-traumatic stress disorder in veterans of the Vietnam war; in the late 1980s, clinicians began to realize that the symptoms of people with borderline and other severe personality disorders could in many ways be understood as manifestations of long-term PTSD. These books go some way to reclaiming the ground and restoring the balance that psychoanalysis had lost during most of this century.

Working with the effects of childhood trauma is deeply disturbing. Both therapist and writer become traumatized. The Scharffs comment in their introduction:

As writers we procrastinated, studied anything else and wrote other books first, because recording our countertransference reawakened the memory of our reception of the patient's trauma. As therapists, and then as writers, we have felt nauseated, anguished, frightened, guilty and helpless.

Having identified and overcome their resistance, the Scharffs have managed to write a truly excellent book, commendable particularly for its breadth and balance. Drawing on their extensive previously published work, the authors give particular emphasis to the relevance of Fairbairn whose thinking was always more attuned than most of his analytic colleagues to the impact of childhood trauma. If one book were to be chosen as a foundation text for the therapy of the traumatized it could well be this one.

Val Richards

Val Richards

London

Val Richards  

In grappling with the rich complexities of this text, I was reminded of a passage in Dostoievsky's Diary of a Writer (1873) which vividly illustrates the operation of the so-called ‘restricted code’ where, such is the rapport between members of the designated group, that the repetition of the same single (unprintable) noun by each in turn, with varying tones and inflexions, conveys a world of meaning and, concludes Dostoievsky, ‘without uttering a single other word, they repeated that one beloved word six times in a row, one after another, and understood one another completely’.

For me, Rhode's rhapsody in blue covers has a similar effect in that its associative mode is seemingly addressed to a select band of cognoscenti for whom the links in a process of thought, essential for the mediation of meaning, are suppressed, apparently deemed unnecessary, producing the impression of a private soliloquy.

The source of this difficulty in communication might possibly also lie in the intense subjective reality for Rhode of the concept of ‘positions’ and the ‘threshold’ between them, almost ignoring the fact that these terms began life as descriptive metaphors for observed clinical phenomena rather than as experiential absolutes. Yet it is as virtually concrete realities that they appear in Rhode's treatment, with the mushrooming of a complex accompanying mythology, so tortuous, so esoteric that, no matter how well accredited and researched, it is hard to imagine such material becoming the stuff of meaningful communications to the patients described. And it is perhaps ironical that the most fascinating parts of the book are those which explore and expose the ancient antecedents of the symbolic in the form of signs, as opposed to symbols, idols as opposed to icons, masks as opposed to faces, and the anti-symbolic nature of the fetish. Thus Rhode broadens our understanding of the deadly lure of the literal, while actual communication is somehow immured in the concrete of the paranoid/schizoid.

Psychotherapy with the Orthodox Jew by Herbert Strean. Published by Jason Aronson, New Jersey/London, 1994; 179 pages; $30.00.

Howard Cooper

Howard Cooper

AGIP, London

Howard Cooper  

For Freud, religious belief was a childish illusion: wishing to feel supported or protected by an all-knowing, all-powerful parent, we invest deities, rituals and religious beliefs with power and authority. Such attempts to console ourselves for an original helplessness are symptoms of a refusal to grow up: ‘Men cannot remain children for ever; they must in the end go out into hostile life’ (The Future of an Illusion, 1927). (Yet what does it mean for a man to state unequivocally, axiomatically, that life is ‘hostile’?)

Freud's hostility to religious belief pervaded much of the analytic literature until quite recently. Practitioners were prone either to interpret religious belief as neurotic, irrational or obsessional (which we know it can be), or else to regard it as a private concern (like political affiliation) to be kept outside the boundaries of analytic investigation. But as psychoanalytically-informed therapy has metamorphosed, particularly in the last 15 years, the focus of the analyst's interest has changed. No longer is the question about a patient's religious belief: ‘Is that true?’ but ‘What in your personal history disposes you to believe that?’ As Adam Phillips puts it, ‘from a psychoanalytic point of view, belief changes from being a question about the qualities of the object of belief, to a question about the history of the subject, the believer’.

But this approach, as Herbert Strean (Director of the New York Center for Psychoanalytic Training) makes clear in his intermittently illuminating book, requires the analyst to be particularly alert to his or her countertransference responses to a patient's religious beliefs and practices. He reports strong negative countertransference feelings amongst his supervisees (Jewish and non-Jewish), and one of the strengths of this book is his disarming capacity to discuss the discomforting feelings evoked in him by certain patients.

Although he only alludes to this in passing, Dr Strean is drawing attention to the possibility that, because of the antipathy of the ‘infidel Jew’ Freud towards his own religion, the earlier generations of analysts (Jews, of course, being over-represented amongst them) retained a nexus of unconscious bias towards the whole phenomenon of religious belief and practice. His book is a plea to analytic therapists to re-examine their assumptions when working with patients who strictly adhere to traditional beliefs and customs: although focused on Orthodox Jews, his argument has a wider provenance, opening up issues relevant to work with, for example, Roman Catholics and Muslims.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

On the face of it, it looks as if the central place of sexuality in psychoanalytic theory has been eroded away together with the shift from phallocentrism to matrocentrism over the course of the century. It is startling to think that a theory firmly founded on biology, the libido and psychosexual stages leading to genitality could evolve into something apparently so different, focused on the infant-mother relation and a life and death drive. What has happened to infant sexuality, or adolescent and adult sexuality for that matter, as major factors in psychopathology? Can sex have become, in our liberated culture, something we take for granted, or so peripheral as to be marginalized out of the picture of psychoanalytic concerns, giving precedence, perhaps, to issues around aggression?

From a number of viewpoints within psychoanalysis sexuality remains central, notably seen as essential in theories about hysteria and perversion. For the BJP 1995 Annual Lecture last October, Juliet Mitchell and Estela Welldon teamed up to speak about these areas, locating the source of symptoms and personality disturbance in sexual conflict and anxiety. It seems to me that further effort to develop and enrich our understanding of mature sexuality needs to be made, in order to round out and articulate a fully fledged object relations theory, perhaps following the lead of Ethel Spector Person on romantic love and Otto Kernberg on the erotic.

In the first paper in this issue, Alan Lidmila writes about the term ‘psychodynamic’, employed so ambiguously and often politically. He suggests a more precise reformulation of the term that recognizes the diversity of analytic practice. The next paper looks at how psychoanalytic concepts have permeated our language to create clusters of meaning. Moving into the area of discourse analysis, Ian Parker relates the way in which psychoanalysis has entered postmodern culture and language in the form of ‘discursive complexes’, organized systems of meaning that construct objects and determine realities. He focuses on three of the ‘discursive complexes’ originating in the therapeutic that have shaped postmodern culture: intellectualization, transference and trauma.

Methods of Identifying Conspicuous Countertransference Reactions

Rolf Holmqvist

Rolf Holmqvist

S-581 83 Linkoping, Sweden

Rolf Holmqvist  

In order to understand the significance of countertransference reactions, it is important to separate unexpected and unusual therapist reactions from those that are normal and expected. In this paper, two different perspectives on how to estimate the unusualness of countertransference reactions are presented. The first method compares professionally expected reactions with professionally unexpected reactions. The second method uses the recurrent reaction pattern of the therapist and the recurrent reaction pattern towards the patient to sort out countertransference reactions that can be considered as unusual. The data for the analysis consists of answers by milieu therapists on a check-list about feelings for patients. The comparison between the methods shows that it is misleading to evaluate a countertransference reaction against a common professional norm. Only when the habitual patterns of therapist and patients are used as norms is it possible to assess the significance of the countertransference reaction.
