The British Journal of Psychotherapy on the Internet

Chris Evans

Chris Evans

Chris Evans  

Since 26 October 1995 information about the BJP has been mounted on the Internet as part of the ‘World Wide Web’. I have mounted the contents page, the editorial, the instructions to authors, subscribers and advertisers and the credits page. I started with volume 12(1) and have just mounted 12(2) in the same way. The information is mounted at:

http://www.sghms.ac.uk/mhs/psychotherapy/jrnls/bjpsycho/intro.htm

I imagine that some readers will have some very clear sense of what this means and may be perfectly capable of typing that address into a computer and browsing through the information there. Others may have a sense that the Internet is something desperately hyped and rather widely denigrated, might be wondering about pathological manic, projective and dissociative processes and feel that this is a topic of no interest to them. I hope there are a number between these extremes who feel some scepticism but may want to read on.

The Internet came into being when the American military realized that the electromagnetic pulse from an aerial nuclear explosion would devastate most solid state hardware over a large area. They decided the answer was to develop a network of computers obeying a very simple routing system for messages ensuring that messages would find their own way from the sending computer to the target computer as long as some proportion of the plethora of possible interconnections through any number of any other computers between were still intact. The system boils down roughly to an agreement to pass on to someone else any message that is not for you. This idea was grabbed with enthusiasm by academic computing centres in the USA and a number of other countries, and soon national networks of academic computers were connected together with commercial and military networks giving the capacity to send electronic mail messages to people anywhere else on that ‘inter-network’ (hence ‘Internet’). The costs were, at least initially, underwritten by central academic funding institutions, by the military or by computing firms eager to capitalize on the resulting developments in networking expertise. The system had a very anarchic feel to it with no centralized controlling organizations and with much of the software and documentation that made it workable being placed in the ‘public domain’ (i.e. not copyright). Despite, and because of, this anarchic organization and generosity, the system actually worked extremely well and grew markedly.

Response to ‘Does psychotherapy need NVQs?’ by Rosemary Randall

Margaret Smith

Margaret Smith

Smithdown Road, Liverpool L15 2LF

Margaret Smith  

Rosemary Randall (1995) has painted a very black and white picture of the difference between the role of the UKCP in ensuring that psychotherapists are competent to practise psychotherapy, and the NVQ Draft Standards for Counselling published in a final version in April 1995. While I agree with her that the language of NVQs is offputting, I feel that perhaps we, as people who live in glass houses ourselves, should not throw stones. We ourselves use off-putting terms such as ‘paranoid-schizoid position’, ‘penis envy’ and ‘unconscious fantasy’ as part of the vocabulary we apply to patients and their relationships.

I personally found the experience of being involved in the trials of the Draft Standards as a thought-provoking and invigorating experience. The task we were set was to think about (a) what it was we really do in offering counselling and therapy, (b) what is best practice in the field, and (c) how could someone else decide whether what a counsellor or therapist was doing lived up to an appropriate standard of competence? Stelzer (1987) suggests that students in training in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis select themselves because of their narcissistic need to be used by people with intense narcissistic needs, and that they have developed very sensitive antennae, enabling them to be empathic with other people, in the same way that they have been ‘hypersensitive to their parents' needs in the past’. Stelzer goes on to say that they will also have a need to fit in ‘as trainees in an institute which they must please, in order to succeed and gain acceptance within the “psychoanalytic family”’ (pp. 63-4). My hypothesis here is that this need to comply while being necessarily trained will usually lead to taking practices on board as a matter of faith, rather than a clearly thought through position about what is good practice. Although far from perfect, I would suggest that the lists that the Draft Standards contain could be used as a chance to rethink practice in the light of experience.

Freud and the Politics of Psychoanalysis by Jose Brunner. Published by Blackwell, Oxford, 1995; 238 pages; £40.00.

Sue Gerhardt

Sue Gerhardt

Oxford

Sue Gerhardt  

Jose Brunner makes the claim that ‘psychoanalysis is political’. In this book he investigates psychoanalytic ideas, language, clinical practice, and the setting of psychoanalysis, taking psychoanalysis as a ‘domain’ within which power is distributed and exercised. Within this domain, Brunner explores such diverse topics as hysteria, shell shock, Freud's metapsychology, the seduction theory, Freud's clinical practice, Freud's Jewishness and the Oedipus complex - all with ‘power relations’ in mind.

Along the way, Brunner raises many fascinating issues. He describes how Freud was prepared to challenge the medical establishment of his day, and its view both of hysterical women in the 1890s and shell-shocked soldiers in 1916. Freud rejected the prevailing idea of hereditary hysteria and ‘degeneracy’, and also rejected the brutal treatments that such patients had been subjected to. He listened to what patients were saying and understood their behaviour as driven by the unconscious not by malingering or selfish motives. Brunner demonstrates how class and gender politics might have come into this. Freud's early patients were often extremely rich and welleducated women with a higher social status than himself, who hired him to provide a service; perhaps he was more motivated to listen to them than Charcot was to listen to the hysterical working-class women who attended the Salpetriere.

Brunner also argues that, although Freud discovered that such symptoms had meaning, his interpretations remained individual ones. Elizabeth von R had incapacitated legs because she could not move forward psychically in her life; soldiers were incapacitated because they could not admit their fears. Freud did not depict such behaviour as a protest against the social powerlessness of women or army conscripts, as Brunner and others (notably feminist writers) prefer to interpret hysteria. Freud's aim as a doctor was to help the patient to recover from his or her symptoms in order to return to their powerless social roles. Soldiers might become well enough after analysis to return to the front to be killed, rich women emotionally strengthened to continue their restricted and frustrating lives with better grace.

Rosemary Gordon  

James Astor has succeeded in rendering in a lively, animated and very readable way the history and personality of Michael Fordham. He gives a clear account of Fordham's contributions to Jung's work and to his theoretical formulations and also conveys something of Jung, the man. Finally he presents the story of analytical psychology from its origins to our own day. This is indeed a formidable achievement carried out by Astor in an economical and very engaging style.

550

The prologue to this book is particularly interesting. Astor concentrates there on the beginning and the ending of the Freud-Jung collaboration, on what brought them together and what separated them. He also clarifies some of the facts that have not always been properly appreciated. For instance, how many of us have really been aware, as John Kerr has pointed out, that at first it was Freud who had needed the international prestige of Bleuer, Jung and the Zurich medical school so as to gain wider recognition and acceptance? And how many have remembered and reflected on the fact that Jung reacted to the break-up with Freud by becoming so deeply distressed that he feared he might suffer a complete psychotic breakdown? Freud's reaction was very different; he founded and organized a secret committee whose purpose it was to marginalize the Zurich group, to guard against any future deviations from Freud's views, and to drown by a flood of counter-publications whatever position Jung took or published. Indeed all who were - and were considered to be - loyal to Freud would not from now on even read Jung. Astor points out that this was the actual professional climate when Fordham began his work in London.

Michael Fordham, as James Astor emphasizes in various ways, was really always ‘Jungian’; this is shown by his immersion in and understanding of Jung's ideas. But his love of analysis and of all studies of the development of the mind prevented him from allowing himself to be restricted by the disagreements of the pioneers.

Simon du Plock

Simon du Plock

London

Simon du Plock  

Paul Ricoeur is hailed as possibly the most influential of the New Freudians who emerged in France in the late 1950s to recast our reading of psychoanalysis and,

143

specifically, to provide a fresh perspective by way of hermeneutics on Freud's seminal texts. Ricoeur will perhaps prove to be a more profound influence on our understanding of Freud in the new millennium than even Lacan, whose repeated stabs a brule pourpoint at American ego psychology inflicted superficial wounds. His work is hardly less difficult than Lacan's, but there is much to be gained by the tenacious and linguistically aware reader, as his considerable impact on the whole area of the humanities, not just textual analysis, psychoanalysis and the phenomenologies of Husserl and Jaspers, attests.

This new book is grounded strongly in the series of talks which constituted the Gifford Lectures ‘On Selfhood: The Question of Personal Identity’ which Ricoeur gave in 1986 at the University of Edinburgh. It also emerges from, and refers back to, his major three-volume Time and Narrative and, while we are provided with a gloss on this along the way, Ricoeur does assume familiarity with his earlier writings. The reader had better also approach Oneself as Another with a reasonable understanding of psychoanalysis, hermeneutics and phenomenology and the relationship between all three, in particular Ricoeur's tracing of the interplay between Freud's ‘energetics’ and his ‘hermeneutics’, that is to say, ‘between his neurobiological, quasi-physical metapsychology of drive and energy and his psychological, quasi-linguistic interpretation of dreams and symptoms’. It should be clear by now that this can in no sense be considered an introductory text.

Nevertheless it does provide the most accessible outline of his ‘philosophical ethics’ available and, taking as its focus the concept of personal identity, develops a hermeneutics of the self to arrive, eventually, at an epistemological place ‘situated beyond the alternative of the cogito and of the anticogito’. Ricoeur's phenomenological and structural reading of Freud has provided an invaluable corrective to ego psychology and its attempts to graft scientific status onto Freud. The present volume continues his project of tracing the evolution of cogito and consciousness via the hermeneutic phenomenology of consciousness in order to arrive at a new conception of psychoanalysis as a hermeneutic endeavour.

Some Views on Psychic Reality

R. Horacio Etchegoyen

This paper is based on the Presidential Address given at the end of the San Francisco Congress in August 1995. The author concentrates on discussing the three main Panel presentations on psychic reality from the technical, clinical and theoretical perspectives and in the context of the life cycle. Referring to Grinberg's introduction to the Congress, he reiterates that psychic reality forms the central point from which psychoanalysis can be contemplated. A special mention is given to the Panel on multidisciplinary perspectives of psychic reality, which includes contributions from two well-known philosophers, in connection with the current epistemological status of psychoanalysis in the context of the Congress's main theme. The author concludes by quoting a sonnet, which he feels illustrates the complex dialectic between reality and fantasy, between truth and lies.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis77, 15, 1996

Myth and Madness: A Report of a Psychoanalytic Study of Antisemitism

Mortimer Ostow

This essay reports the findings and conclusions of a psychoanalytic study of antisemitism based upon case reports and classical, historical and literary documents. With respect to antisemitic sentiments, individual dynamics are overridden by stereotypical myths. After the definitive secession of early Jewish and Gentile Christian followers from the Jewish community at the end of the first century Common Era, the Jews were stigmatized and demonized by them and by the early Church fathers and labelled as a principle of evil, along with Satan, that was to blame for all Christian misfortune. The many antisemitic myths that evolved throughout the history of the Christian West all concurred in this theme. Apocalyptic thinking required such a principle as the source of the death phase, so that the elimination of Jews became the condition for the rebirth phase. In the presence of a sense of disorganization and chaos, societies congeal into fundamental groups that require a mythic enemy. These groups tend to cultivate apocalyptic paranoia. Under those circumstances, anti-Jewish sentiment and discrimination become active persecution. The essay, and to a much greater extent, the book upon which it is based, examine some of the findings of the case studies, analyse apocalyptic thinking and describe the psychology of the fundamentalist community.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

In our pluralistic times we have so many different models of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy in existence that it can be difficult to see overall trands, changes or even practices that we all share. It is possible, however, to see a movement in psychoanalytic thinking away from a positivistic scientific model in which insight or clinical fact is discerned by an objective analyst and then delivered to the patient, towards a model in which psychic truth is reached mutually, created by the clinical couple in the ongoing therapeutic dialogue. Paving the pathway to this progression has been the validation and development of the countertransference not only as a communicative function but as representing the contribution and inclusion of the mind of the analyst. This intersubjective view in which the analyst's and patient's subjective responses to each other create symbol and meaning might well cause confusion and alarm, threatening to shake the analyst out of his safe, shadowy neutrality and edging him into a less comfortable, intersubjective spotlight. This anti-authoritarian move would appear to be immensely destabilizing, for who is the ultimate arbiter of the truth when there are disagreements? Yet it is difficult to see the analytic situation as other than an intersubjective project, given that there are two minds at work, or how else to construe the interaction other than as the therapist and patient taking in each other's projections, adding something to them, then giving them back for further elaboration until truth is found - a joint creative effort.

In a paper that takes account of the difficulty in capturing the human subject in all its ‘lawless profusion’, Georgia Lepper offers a research methodology for the therapeutic dialogue that consists of studying the language and discourse of the consulting-room. Discourse analysis, developed in the field of sociology, could be adopted by psychoanalytic research to illuminate the elements of interpretation and therapeutic process, with a potential for examining intersubjective models. Lepper calls for those who are interested in research to come forward.

Phil Mollon  

This is a timely and very necessary book addressing the clinical implications and complexities of the turmoil over delayed memories of childhood trauma. Relatively little of what has been written prior to this has been clinically sophisticated, presenting issues and arguments that are meaningful and plausible to the practising psychotherapist. By contrast, all the papers in this collection are excellent and of direct relevance to the clinician and therapist.

The editor, Judith Alpert, is a psychoanalyst and also co-chair of the APA Working Group on Evaluation of Memories of Childhood Abuse. She provides a very lucid and perceptive account of the scientific, social, political and professional context of the debate - and one does need to appreciate the context in order to grasp what this is all about. This is then followed by three papers on psychological science including a very good review by van der Kolk on the psychobiology of the trauma response and the long-term biological imprints of childhood disturbance. Two other papers on hypnosis and suggestibility are comprehensive and valuable.

The bulk of the book consists of eight chapters looking at psychoanalytic dimensions of memory and self-knowledge as perceived in the consulting-room. These cover such issues as: the effect of abuse on memory and the organization of the self, the fate of imagination in those who are incestuously abused in childhood, disturbances in the sense of time, transference and countertransference with the abused, the impact of validation of recovered memories. All these are sensitive and thought-provoking explorations of complex areas which are pervaded by ambiguity and paradox.

Sue Grand, in her chapter ‘Incest and the intersubjective politics of knowing history’, draws upon Orwell's 1984 to illustrate the kind of ‘doublethink’ and ‘tampering with reality’ that may take place in an incestuous family.

David Smith

David Smith

London

David Smith  

The Cosmic Circle is an accessible introduction to the quantitative research into the psychoanalytic process undertaken by Robert Langs and Anthony Badalamenti over the last decade. Langs established a reputation as an innovative and controversial psychoanalytic thinker before collaborating with Badalamenti, a mathematician, to

285

investigate features of psychotherapeutic interactions formally. Many readers acquainted with his views on psychoanalytic technique and the structure of the mind remain ignorant of the nature and results of this research. One reason for this is that the research is couched in terms derived from mathematics and physics which many psychotherapists (including myself) find forbidding. Even if one succeeds in understanding an investigation and its outcome, this territory is so alien to most of us that it is difficult to evaluate what these authors have so painstakingly presented. Another reason is that many psychotherapists do not understand how this research bears on their clinical practice. It is this point that I wish to take up in the present review. Although I am shamefully ignorant of both mathematics and physics, I think that the research undertaken by Langs and Badalamenti is both significant and relevant to anyone concerned with the growth of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. In order to explain why this is the case, I will first need to discuss aspects of the history and philosophy of psychology and the relationship between psychoanalysis and natural science.

In creating psychoanalysis, Sigmund Freud tried to develop a science of mental life. Trained as a neuroscientist during the final quarter of the nineteenth century, Freud was deeply influenced by the growing scientific consensus that mental states are intimately bound up with the functioning of the central nervous system and that the. central nervous system itself is explicable purely in terms of the laws of physics and chemistry. In short, Freud believed that the mind is a part of nature, and it was this philosophical naturalism that underpinned his psychoanalytic theories.

Science, Transference and the Unconscious

Karl Figlio

Karl Figlio

24 Rosebery Avenue, Colchester COl 2UJ

Karl Figlio  

There is a contradiction at the root of psychoanalysis. While it aims to be a science, it is dedicated to freedom. And since the psychoanalytic process struggles towards such a condition, there is a contradiction in the method as well. It is a process with patterns and predictable moments, but with a gap between them and the freedom towards which it aims. The notions of a causal gap and of freedom challenge the idea that psychoanalysis is a science, but also highlight its prime feature: the notion of an essential contradiction.

I have two aims in this paper. Firstly, I argue that psychoanalysis is built on such a paradox: the unconscious is irrational rather than just unrecognized or repudiated, and the psyche is essentially contradictory or dialectical. Secondly, I aim to show that psychoanalytic method and research are sensitive to the models we choose of the psyche, and that there is always a risk that, the better the model, in the sense of being readily applied, the less it approximates to the dialectical nature of the psyche.

One attempt to dissolve the apparent contradiction at the heart of psychoanalysis is not to notice it - to relegate the contradictory moments to separate, noncommunicating aspects of Freud's mind and of our minds. We attribute his deterministic thinking to nineteenth-century science, displayed in his metapsychological writings; and that on freedom to his clinical work, displayed in his case histories. We then think of ourselves either as scientists or as clinicians.1

The views of nature, of science and of philosophy that were current in Freud's time do not bear out this interpretation. Leading scientific ideas of nature were built on the failure of simple mechanical models, on paradox and on the inadequacy of commonsense. The reductive mechanical approach of the ‘physicalist school’ of the mid-nineteenth century, usually associated with Hermann von Helmholtz, Carl Ludwig, Ernst Brucke and Emil du-Bois Reymond, had given way to a sceptical empiricism, in which concepts were useful tools - even conventions - rather than assertions about the fundamental stuff of nature. Space itself, the frame of nature, was no longer thought to be linear and three dimensional; the notion of causal linkages between events had become probabilistic; and the quantum world was built on impossible events, such as the movement of particles between two positions without existing anywhere in between. Nature, at its root, was free, or at least indeterminate, and certainly not pinned down by commonsense.2

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale  

Having the conviction, as we do, that all of our human experience is composed of a mixture of reality and fantasy, how do we as therapists look upon memories that emerge in the process of psychotherapy? What is their historical status and truth value, of particular importance when the memories involve possible immoral or criminal actions from the past? This issue includes a special section prepared by Ann Scott on recovered memories of sexual abuse. She has brought together the views of an analytic psychotherapist, Fiona Gardner, with a review of the literature by Bessel van der Kolk and Rita Fisler from American sources where the recovered memory debate is more widespread. This review encompasses the nature of traumatic memory and amnesia in general, and PTSD in particular. It is introduced by Sandra Bloom who has been involved in the recovered memory debate for a number of years from the clinical and socio-historical aspects. In this section we have a response to these two papers by Professor John Morton, a cognitive psychology researcher on memory and co-author of the British Psychological Society position paper on recovered memories of sexual abuse.

Has an overriding emphasis on the transference eclipsed the notion of working alliance in modern-day analytic therapy? In a reappraisal of the concept of working alliance, Charlotte Wynn Parry and Diana Birkett look at attitudes towards it from the point of view of different schools and pick out Greenson's position as the most useful, arguing that the concept of working alliance is valuable for our practice and should not be overlooked. Next, we have an exploration of separation from the mother, couched in the context of Kristeva's ‘necessity of matricide’, presented in a paper by Christina Wieland. Without this symbolic murder in the service of individuation and development, melancholia and depression result, according to the Lacanian framework, and the ‘law of the father’ is not established in psychic reality. Wieland suggests a less violent solution in which the mother is not banished into the unconscious to reign as a bad object or lost traumatically, but allowed to exist as part of an internal couple by gradually working through oedipal anxieties.

Mental Space by Salomon Resnik. Published by Karnac Books, London 1995; 120 pages; £15.00.

Jane Kitto

Jane Kitto

LCP, London

Jane Kitto  

Once, as we were sitting in the cafe, we debated the difference between ‘mental space’, ‘internal world’ and ‘psychic apparatus’. We concluded that it would be impossible to sp eakof an internal world without the concept of mental space. And ‘psychic apparatus’? To this, Anna Resnik answered: ‘The mind is the all-purpose crank-handle’.

This is a lovely book, original without being idiosyncratic, personal without being sentimental. Salomon Resnik trained in Buenos Aires and encountered the international psychoanalytic world first at the Geneva congress of 1955, at which Bion presented an early paper on schizophrenic thought. He determined to come to Britain, which he did via Paris, to study with Klein, Rosenfeld and others, subsequently working in Paris and Italy. While Resnik's ideas spring from the Kleinian tradition, his thinking and writing are also formed by the Continental tradition with its roots in philosophical questions. This marrying of the almost philosophy-free English tradition and the sometimes obstruse and over-philosophical Continental (and particularly French) tradition underlines the extent to which philosophical questions are at the root of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

Resnik tells us that this book arose out of seminars he gave in Paris, often followed by discussions in a nearby cafe. The idea of mental space is itself a philosophical conundrum since the mind is non-spatial; yet, as Resnik points out in the above quotation, we cannot manage without it. Those who want to pursue the philosophical aspects of this problem are referred to the book of the same title by Robert Young. Resnik instead studies how the idea of space emerges in psychoanalytic practice. Each chapter heading introduces a new aspect of space: ‘A space for psychoanalysis’, ‘A space for thinking’, ‘A space for dreaming’, etc.

Resnik aims to ‘invite you into my workshop’, not only through clinical material but by reflecting on his experience as analyst. The reader will get an idea of what it is like for this analyst to work with these patients. ‘Reaching out from oneself towards the other always entails a risk: interpersonal contact is indispensable but hazardous’, hence he devotes his first chapter to the setting for the work.

Commentary by a Psychoanalyst, Member of the Independent Group

Leon Kleimberg

Leon Kleimberg

9 Dunstan Road, London NW 11 8AG

Leon Kleimberg  

It is difficult to make comments on other therapists' work. Even more so when it is at a distance and in writing. Assuming these limitations and the injustice done to the therapeutic process, I am going to try to do the task that has being asked of me in the fairest way possible.

Reading the case notes, the first idea that comes to my mind is that I wished I had been given a better and more detailed history of the patient. For example, relationships with parents and siblings, psycho-sexual development, inner psychological state of mind, childhood neurosis, schooling, etc. - in other words, some more material that would help to build up a better picture of this patient and her internal world. I agree with the therapist's description that the presenting complaint was a reactive depression in relation to work, nevertheless it is interesting to note that later on, as the process of therapy unfolds, an underlying claustrophobic anxiety in relation to work is also revealed.

I am sure that the session material, in many ways, is full of unconscious material and communications, as, for example, dynamics of relationships with men, relationships with women, power issues, maternity issues, feelings for father and mother, destructiveness, reparation, deceit, and so on, that I will not try to explore now. I will just try to address what seems to me an important clinical and technical difficulty when one is confronted with the task of treating gender identity problems. Patients with gender identity conflicts usually come, consciously or unconsciously, with the wish to address only a particular focalized problem such as, in this instance, work-related issues. The point I would like to make here is that when patients with this kind of problem project their inner conflicts to the outside world, it becomes extremely difficult to try to link the externalized problem with the intra-psychic gender identity issues and with the transference to the therapist. In the material presented the initial sysmptom, depression in relation to work, shifted to claustrophobic anxieties to work, yet when any attempts by the therapist to link them with the therapy were made, the patient dropped it or moved back to the work environment. In my view, these are signs of how threatening the patient finds it to explore these anxieties in relation to the therapist, to her partner, to her parents or to her inner world. The material in this respect can be understood as depressive and claustrophobic anxiety that the patient is feeling in relation to her inner world and her inner object relationships.

The Future of an Empirical Psychoanalysis'

Peter Fonagy PHD

Peter Fonagy

Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT

Peter Fonagy  

Is Psychoanalysis a Science?

There are many big questions for which fortunately we do not feel compelled to find answers. What caused the French Revolution? Is there an afterlife? I categorize into this family: ‘Is psychoanalysis a science?’ The category may be designated as questions for people with too much leisure time, formulated in an inherently unproductive mould.

Yet psychoanalysts seem to care what the appropriate answer to the question might be. A more interesting question would be, why should they care? We care because science brings credibility. As Paul Meehl (1995) put it, ‘science has the best attested knowledge claims’ in our culture. Objective, trustworthy knowledge which most closely approximates what people regard as ‘true’ or ‘real’. Many disciplines make such claims including theology, metaphysics, politics, literary criticism, philosophy, journalism, aesthetics, but scientific observations are simply taken more seriously than claims from any of these other domains. That this is indisputably so is marked by our language: ‘scientifically speaking’ sounds compelling (whereas ‘journalistically speaking’ somehow does not carry the same implication).

Why should people regard science as a preferred route to knowledge? The answer might be in the methods that scientists use, perhaps embodied in guidelines rather than in principles. Amongst the key features are an attitude of scepticism, the repeatability of observations and, often, that these should be accessible to mathematical and statistical tools.

It is clear that clinical psychoanalysis falls far short of such desiderata. For example, there is no coherent set of principles that could define psychoanalysis as a singular treatment, which is the minimum requirement for replicability. Even in Glover's (1940, unpublished) survey of psychoanalytic technique in the 1930s, the heterogeneity of psychoanalytic technique was very evident and, as we know, matters have not improved since. In fact, a relatively easily defensible position may be that psychoanalysis cannot be defined by its theory, and those who wish to commune under this banner share but a relatively superficial set of priorities. These include practising the most intensive long-term psychotherapeutic treatment acceptable to the culture, using the couch and imposing a harsh regimen of abstinence on their patients and themselves.

The Treatment of the Borderline Patient: Applying Fairbairn's Object Relations Theory in the Clinical Setting by David P. Celani. Published by International Universities Press, 1993; 188 pages; $28.50.

Eleanore Perlman

Eleanore Perlman

London

Eleanore Perlman  

Celani's book is based on the difficulties he encountered with ‘borderline’ patients addicted to frustrating, rejective relationships with either their actual parents or with significant others. Such patients seem immune to relationships with better objects. Sadly they may also seem immune to classical psychoanalytic technique.

The book is valuable for its clear exposition of Fairbairn's account of the development of internalization, splitting and secondary repression, but the main emphasis is not metapsychology. Fairbairn's challenge to the Freudian paradigm, as developed by Celani, also challenges the prevailing assumptions about ‘proper’ psychoanalytic technique. As yet, the implications of Fairbairn's interpersonal, developmental model of the emergent self have been little explored and, given the relative neglect of his theory, I provide a sketchy summary.

For Fairbairn, the persistent feature underlying the varying symptomatology of borderline personality is infantile dependence. Celani agrees with Fairbairn's premise of a fundamental need for acceptance. In proportion to the failure to meet and acknowledge this basic self-need, the child will internalize the too-frustrating relationship, making it more amenable to psychological control. If the condition of infantile dependence persists, the child, and then the ‘borderline’ adult, cannot reject the unsatisfactory object. The strength of the undercurrent of need blocks separation and individuation. The immature self cannot encompass the loss of hope for a good relationship with the original object.

Frustration excites and intensifies need but also exacerbates rage and hatred. To solve this dilemma of ambivalence the internalized object is split, and this splitting carries over to a splitting of the nascent self. This promotes ego distortion because it gives rise to three ego structures each relating to three respective internalized objects. The needy libidinal self relates to the exciting object. The anti-libidinal self relates to the rejecting object, often on a basis of identification. These two relationships are repressed. The central ego relates to the accepted object which retains the core of the amenable features of the original object. The central ego then adapts as best it can to external reality, but this is a reality sanitized of its excessively frustrating and persecutory features. This process protects the relationship with the external parent as well as the relationship with the internalized ‘good’ object.

Unconscious Logic: An Introduction to Matte Blanco's Bi-Logic and its Uses by Eric Rayner. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 1994.

Ross Skelton

Ross Skelton

Dublin

Ross Skelton  

The morning I discovered Matte Blanco I had just finished giving a lecture on logic and was leafing through the psychotherapy journals when I chanced on the review of a book with the improbable title of The Unconscious as Infinite Sets. I had always thought that my dual interests of psychotherapy and logic were irreconcilable and had long kept them separate. But this book was to teach me that logic could illuminate

278

clinical problems in psychotherapy. Now at last we have a good introduction to Matte Blanco's ideas written by Eric Rayner which makes this very different psychoanalytic perspective relatively easy to understand. He explains new concepts step by step but, more importantly, he gives many clinical illustrations of logical ideas. But firstly, who is Matte Blanco?

Matte Blanco was a British-trained Chilean psychoanalyst and psychiatrist with a special interest in schizophrenia, and most of his startling clinical examples come from work with psychotic patients. His initial article ‘Expression in symbolic logic of the characteristics of the system Ucs’ (which appeared in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis in 1959) directly links his theory to what he calls ‘schizophrenic thinking’. His most original idea is that the mind operates two logics at the same time. This double process is called ‘Bi-logic’. One logic is our customary bivalent logic which he calls asymmetric, and the other is the ambi-valent logic of the dream which he calls symmetric. The two kinds of logic characterize two kinds of being: symmetrical being which approximates the timeless, changeless world of Parmenides, and asymmetrical being which approximates the spatio-temporal flux of everyday life. In all our mental processes both forms of being are co-present but distinct and irreconcilable. Now how can this bi-logic and philosophy be useful clinically?

Rayner begins his account with Freud who, in the Rat Man case, recalls a case from earlier days. The patient, Freud noted, always had brand new banknotes. He explained that it was a matter of conscience with him not to hand over dirty notes because they harboured dangerous bacteria and might harm the recipient. It emerges that this patient masturbates very young girls with his hand. Freud remarks: ‘But aren't you afraid of doing her some harm, fiddling about with her genitals with your dirty hand?’ The man flares up because Freud has undone the displacement of the ‘dirty handling’ from the girls' genitals to the banknotes. Rayner's point here is that genitals and notes are logically equivalent with respect to both being ‘handleable’. To put it more conventionally: banknotes and girls' genitals (for this abuser) were members of the same class - the class of ‘handleable objects’. This is the key to understanding Matte Blanco - that the unconscious mind sees many physical objects as equivalent in a way that the conscious mind does not. Thus the displacement must take place from one object to another in virtue of some consciously or unconsciously perceived similarity. This process is called by him ‘generalization’.

This article traces the development of Sandor Ferenczi's conviction that patients' analytic material might be understood, in part, as a valid unconscious portrayal and critique of the way their analyses were being conducted. Jan Wiener  

The paper focuses on the ways in which many analysts have neglected their conscious and unconscious feelings about money to the detriment of their own individuation in this area. The authors highlight reasons why there is a tendency to project most of the pathology about money onto patients and emphasize the failure of training institutions to provide adequate conditions in which their members can reflect upon and integrate their money complexes. Using two clinical vignettes where money was a central issue between analyst and patient, the usefulness of Jung's concept of the shadow is illustrated. The activation of the mercurial collective aspects of the shadow which promote the avoidance of consciousness in relation to money is explored.

1 Sexuality and Psychoanalysis: Hysteria

Juliet Mitchell

Juliet Mitchell

Juliet Mitchell  

Perversion and hysteria are two of the main dimensions of sexuality within psychoanalysis. In 1926 in Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety, Freud, foreshadowing the development of object relations orientation in future psychoanalytic work, cautioned against losing sight of the importance of sexuality. Following the First World War and the formulation of a death drive in conflict with a life drive, there was a new emphasis on primal anxiety and on the helplessness of the human infant who is dependent for a long time on another person for the satisfaction of all its vital needs. Freud re-emphasized the sexual dimension of narcissism for the ego struggling with dependence, and stressed that it was not helplessness itself but the protosexual needs of the oral, anal and phallic drives that the human being needed to have satisfied by the other person. Despite this emphasis, sexuality did come to play a diminishing role in the later development of psychoanalytic theory. With one important, if time-limited, exception - the many discussions of female sexuality in the late 1920s to the mid- 1930s - sexuality largely evacuated the centre of the psychoanalytic arena. Recently, Andre Green has asked: ‘Whatever has happened to sexuality in psychoanalysis?’ and made a plea for its return.

Tonight Estela Welldon is going to talk about perversion and I am going to look at hysteria. Perversion and hysteria in Freud's early work were seen as two sides of the same coin, a sort of flip. It was likely that, if you were a hysteric, you would be a woman; if you were perverse you would be a man. Perversion was connected with masculinity, hysteria with femininity. Within the same family you would often have siblings where the brother would be perverse and the sister would be hysterical. These were the very earliest days, the 1880s and 1890s, when psychoanalysis was emerging as a clinical practice and as a theory. These two areas led to two dominant texts of the early period of psychoanalysis. Perversion and the study of perversions led to the Three Essays on Sexuality (Freud 1905a) with the whole notion of the pregenital and the polymorphously perverse, and really a new understanding both of inversion (that is, homosexuality) and of perversion (that is, the enactment of pregenital sexualities). I would argue that hysteria, in a rather strange way, led to the other major text of the foundation of psychoanalysis - The Interpretation of Dreams (Freud 1900), which has much more about hysteria in it than one thinks on a first reading. Both dreams and hysterical symptoms are understood as wish fulfilments. For a time after this dreams and hysteria became completely intertwined so that the main text that people think of in Freud's writing as the text par excellence about hysteria, ‘Dora: a fragment of a case of hysteria’ (Freud 1905b), is, of course, an analysis of two of Dora's dreams.

Katherine Killick

Katherine Killick

Second floor, 16 Chequer Street, St Albans AL1 3YD

Katherine Killick  

This paper draws on material from six years of psychotherapeutic work with a schizophrenic patient in the environment of an art therapy department in a large psychiatric hospital. The author discusses the material with particular reference to the work of Bick, Bion and Meltzer. She proposes that the analytically informed art psychotherapy setting came to constitute a containing object for the patient's unintegrated state of mind. This enabled a shift from intrusive identification to projective identification to take place in his use of the therapist and the setting. The substances and objects in the setting helped to absorb the violence of intrusive identifications which defended against the catastrophic anxieties overwhelming his capacity to think when he was acutely psychotic. Over time images emerged which were used to communicate with the therapist, and the evolution of one particular image, ‘Sleeping Muse’, is traced. The author proposes that this work was helpful to the patient, and questions whether work of this kind is possible in current psychiatric settings.

Alan Lidmila  

I hope to make a preliminary contribution to the development of a model that more clearly reformulates the practices of psychoanalytic psychotherapy in a way that recognizes a diversity of analytic practice that I think has been misdescribed - technically and politically - as ‘psychodynamic’. The paper firstly considers the question of definition and suggests four identifiable meanings of the term ‘psychodynamic’. The discussion then reviews a number of core and inextricably connected questions of theory and practice under the following headings: setting and regression, time and frequency, countertransference, creativity and the real relationship, interpretation and pure technique, and the problem of eclecticism. The paper concludes by briefly exploring the parameters of psychodynamic practice in relation to eclecticism in psychotherapy, and makes a plea for a model that is consistent, authentic and ecumenical.

Psychotherapy and Science: A Reply to Joseph Schwartz

David Smith

David Smith

London NW1 4NS

David Smith  

I would like to offer a brief reply to Joseph Schwartz's paper ‘Is physics a good model for psychoanalysis? Reflections on Langs and Badalamenti’ (British Journal of Psychotherapy 11(4), pp. 594-600). Schwartz's paper is itself a contribution to a series of papers discussing the work of Langs and Badalamenti (Burgoyne 1994; Harris 1994; Langs & Badalamenti 1994a, 1994b). All too often contentious contributions to the psychotherapeutic literature are politely ignored (I use ‘psychotherapy’ as a generic term inclusive of psychoanalysis). It is refreshing to find that intense and sustained scientific and philosophical debate is encouraged within the pages of this Journal.

Schwartz critizes Langs and Badalamenti on several fronts. Roughly half of Schwartz's paper is taken up with technical comments on their handling of models derived from physics (and applied to psychoanalytic data). Schwartz, a physicist by training, is well equipped to discuss such issues whereas I, in my ignorance of mathematics and physics, am not. I will therefore refrain from commenting on these elements of his paper. Schwartz also provides some ad hominem criticism and some reflections on the issue of the scientificity of psychoanalysis, the latter of which will be my main concern.

On the ad hominem front, Schwartz objects to what he calls the flamboyant and unrestrained tone of Langs and Badalamenti's paper. This is fine as an expression of Schwartz's impatience but carries little cognitive significance. The style and tone of a paper have no intrinsic relationship to the value of its content. In fairness, Schwartz seems to concede this point.

On the philosophical front, Schwartz claims, without any presentation of evidence or any gesture towards providing any supporting argument, that:

For me Langs seems to reify the unconscious - to turn a mental process, the unconscious, into a thing - while at the same time his technique seems to me to have the danger of leaving the client isolated and in an anxious, persecuted state. (p. 597)

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Letchworth

Phil Mollon  

Despite the title's emphasis upon dreams, this is a book about memory, trauma and reconstruction in psychoanalysis. As such, it is both excellent and important.

Share explains that the project began with a patient's dream, dreamed on her birthday, of being given a blue basket. No meaningful associations were produced to ‘blue’, but various features prompted the analyst to wonder aloud whether the patient might have turned blue due to asphyxiation at birth. Although full confirmation of this was never obtained, there was a striking shift in the patient's behaviour following this interpretation, a move from continually enacting life and death scenarios. This led the author to reflect at length on whether very early experiences can be recorded, unconsciously enacted in behaviour and represented in dreams.

She notes that in classical analysis reconstruction of preverbal events was rare but, as analysts have attempted to treat more disturbed patients, interest in preverbal and even neonatal experience has increased. New technology also opens investigatory possibilities. Recently Piontelli's ultrasound studies have shown continuity between pre and postnatal life. In a related example, Piontelli studied a two-year-old psychotic child who was born with the umbilical cord wrapped tightly around her neck; the girl would always wear a heavy chain wrapped around her neck and in the consultingroom would endeavour to wrap herself in the curtain cord.

Some analysts, such as Anna Freud and Donald Spence, have seen the reconstruction of a veridical account of the childhood past as impossible, particularly because of the problem of distinguishing fantasy and actual experience. Share lists eight common arguments against veridical reconstruction. She points out that these problems have tended to lead to (a) a focus on here-and-now transference interpretations and (b) the adoption of a narrative perspective, as advocated by Spence. Share believes that both these solutions are unbalanced and asks how infantile trauma can ever be reached and dealt with, as it may need to be, if interpretations address only the here and now; instead she recommends a moving between past and present, each perspective enriching the other.

Margaret Gardiner

Margaret Gardiner

London

Margaret Gardiner  

Newman's book is built around key words from Winnicott's work. Entries stretch alphabetically from Absolute Dependence to Worst (Not being Seen or Heard is the Worst that Can Happen). They consist of quotations, many of them substantial, from Winnicott, woven together with Newman's own commentary and clinical illustrations. Some entries are quite short, others longer; others are followed by extensions which Newman calls ‘Elaborations’. Each quotation ends with an extremely detailed and useful list of references to the word/concept in Winnicott's writings.

The ‘critical dictionary’ format has become a familiar one to us in our field but, Newman stresses, this book is not that: it is offered, rather, as a kind of ‘portable’ Winnicott - first and foremost a compilation of selected quotations and extracts designed to excite people into reading texts. It is also a celebration of the power of Winnicott's ideas.

The basis of the book is material generated for, and by, regular series of lectures and seminars given by Newman over more than 20 years, beginning soon after Winnicott's death. (Newman was founder of what was later to be christened - at Clare Winnicott's wish - the Squiggle Foundation.) There can be no doubt, from the book, that Newman knows his Winnicott inside out, and is still full of curiosity about his ideas as well as a kind of awe at their power and originality.

Newman sets out to redress what he feels to be some important imbalances in our knowledge of Winnicott's work. Firstly, it is his contention that Winnicott has not actually been widely read: his quiet voice has been drowned out by ‘ambitious and louder mouths insistently intent not only on founding schools and indoctrinating followers, but hell-bent on such strife that little else could be heard above the clamour’ (p. 7). (Newman rarely misses a chance to get in a dig, on Winnicott's behalf, at Klein and her followers.) We remember Masud Khan's observation that it was Winnicott's fate to be ‘politely disregarded’ by his analytic colleagues.

What Do Psychoanalysts Want? The Problem of Aims in Psychoanalytic Therapy by Joseph Sandler and Anna Ursula Dreher. Published by Routledge, London, 1996; 141 pages; £13.99 (paperback).

Faye Carey

Faye Carey

London

Faye Carey  

This very readable book is an impressively simple but finely focused investigation into the persistence of the ironic question of its title. The extension of the question - one which has affected practitioners from Freud onwards - is what do psychoanalysts want from the practice of psychoanalysis: to further theoretical and clinical research, or to cure? Embedded in this is the other chronic query: is psychoanalysis a science, a philosophy or an art? And, whatever its definition, how is ‘success’ measured? The authors, Joseph Sandler and Anna Ursula Dreher, take a chronological approach - dividing the research neatly into decades of thought, and looking at the material from three different perspectives: historical, cultural and clinical.

Freud at first saw psychoanalysis as a cure - the ‘talking cure’ - whose aim was to alleviate the patient's symptoms, at least to the point of ‘transforming hysterical misery into common unhappiness’, or, more cheerfully, to enable the patient to attain a greater capacity ‘to work and to love’. With Freud's scientific ambition for his work, these aims expanded to include a growing variety of more or less measurable criteria. Decade by decade, each chapter traces the development of the various aims and consequent processes of psychoanalysis, and the theories and factions that have grown and split along the way.

From the beginning, conflict existed between the two objectives: Freud's caution regarding furore sanandi, the passion to cure, is set against his statement, ‘it is not a good thing to work on a case scientifically, while treatment is still proceeding’. This duality of purpose is sustained throughout his writings and forms the foundation of the discourse between psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. The authors make clear their own view, however, that those practitioners who continue to think of psychoanalysis as pure science are deceiving themselves, since ‘all analysts are affected by therapeutic aims’.

The book charts the course of psychoanalytic aims through the expanding field of theory, by way of the topographical and structural models of the early days, the development of ego psychology in the US in the 1930s and 1940s, and the fragmentations which took place in the UK alongside the growth of object relations theory in the next decades. Throughout, the dialogue expands and contracts in relation to aims and outcomes, intrapsychic and interpersonal considerations, and the ongoing discussion between analysis and therapy as - almost 50 years on - ‘the tendencies evident in the 1950s continued into the next decade as conceptual tensions which would eventually crystallize into definite schools within the psychoanalytic movement’. The authors see the 1960s as characterized by remarkably contradictory points of view, with ‘a persisting idealization of analysis as a therapeutic method’ on the one hand, alongside a growing sense of realism with regard to its limitations on the other. Both the work and the writing became more specific to individual conditions. Here they point out that ‘the tension cannot be divorced from the profound sociocultural changes of the time’, an insight which applies not only to the turbulent events of the 1960s, but surely to the entire history of psychoanalysis.

Dissociation and the Fragmentary Nature of Traumatic Memories: Overview

Bessel Van Der Kolk and Rita Fisler

Rita Fisler

Rita Fisler  

The nature and reliability of traumatic memories have been controversial issues in psychiatry for over a century. Traumatic memories are difficult to study, since the profoundly upsetting emotional experiences that may give rise to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other trauma related outcomes cannot be approximated in a laboratory setting. For example, even viewing a movie depicting actual executions failed to precipitate post-traumatic symptoms in normal college students (Pitman, personal communication, 1994). If trauma is defined as the experience of an inescapable stressful event that overwhelms one's existing coping mechanisms, it is questionable whether findings of memory distortions in normal subjects exposed to videotaped stresses in the laboratory can serve as meaningful guides to understanding traumatic memories. Clearly, there is little similarity between viewing a simulated car accident on a TV screen, and being the responsible driver in a car crash in which one's own children are killed. While stress evokes homeostatic mechanisms that lead to self-conservation and resource-re-allocation (e.g. Selye 1956), PTSD involves a unique combination of learned conditioning, problems modulating arousal, and shattered meaning propositions. Shalev (1995) has proposed that this complexity is best understood as the co-occurrence of several interlocking pathogenic processes including (a) an alteration of neurobiological processes affecting stimulus discrimination (expressed as increased arousal and decreased attention), (b) the acquisition of conditioned fear responses to trauma-related stimuli, and (c) altered cognitive schemata and social apprehension.

Without the option of inflicting actual trauma in the laboratory, there are limited options for the exploration of traumatic memories. These include collecting retrospective reports from traumatized individuals, post-hoc observations, and provoking, then studying, traumatic memories and flashbacks in people with PTSD. Surprisingly, since the early part of this century, there have been very few published studies that systematically explore the nature of traumatic memories based on detailed patient reports. Provocation studies of traumatic memories in the laboratory have examined psychophysiologic responses to visual or auditory stimuli (e.g. Pitman, Orr, Forgue, de Jong & Claiborn 1987; Rauch et al. 1995), and biological agents have been shown to promote access to trauma-related memories as well (Rainey et al. 1987; Southwick et al. 1993).

Race and Colour in Internal and External Reality

Sami Timimi

Sami Timimi

127 Axminster Road, London N7 6BT

Sami Timimi  

To understand the psychological origins and impact of racism, two assumptions are proposed. The first is that racism develops out of internal paranoid schizoid splits. The second relates to the manner in which these splits are organized. The history of racial exploitation provides powerful projection highways that can be used to maintain these internal splits. Reciprocal projective identification between internal and external white part-objects and internal and external black part-objects locates desirable aspects of the self in white objects and undesirable aspects in black objects. Some of the resulting complex defences and identifications are illustrated using case material.

The Transgenerational Impact of Cultural Trauma: Linking Phenomena in Treatment of Third Generation Survivors of the Holocaust

Gary Winship and Jane Knowles

Jane Knowles

Winterbourne House, 53-55 Argyle Road, Reading, Berkshire RG1 7YL

Jane Knowles  

The long-term impact of the Holocaust is considered with reference to material presented in the case histories of patients treated in an NHS psychotherapy department (West Berkshire). The treatment of three third generation survivors of the Holocaust is described. Insofar as it is only recently that third generation phenomena are emerging, the clinical work is experimental. In the spirit of a greater consideration of the interlace between psychoanalysis and cultural trauma (Hunter Brown 1992), this paper examines the relationship between the magnitude of a cultural trauma (and its resonance) and the time it takes for the trauma to be worked through. The implications for the treatment of survivors of other cultural atrocities, for example, the Hungerford massacre and Dunblane, are considered. A provisional psychodynamic diagnostic axiom is proposed by the authors, and it is hoped that this may be useful for other clinicians.

2 Perversions in Men and Women

Estela Welldon MD

Estela Welldon

Portman Clinic, 8 Fitzjohn's Avenue, London NW3 5NA

Estela Welldon  

Definition of Perversion

Perversion is normally seen as a condition in which a person does not feel free to obtain sexual genital gratification through intimate bodily contact with another person. Instead, he or she feels ‘taken over’ by a compulsive activity which is subjectively experienced as inexplicable and ‘bizarre’ but which provides a release of unbearable and increasing sexual anxiety. The activity usually involves an unconscious desire to harm others or him/herself. Fantasies about bizarre or perverse actions do not qualify as perversion. True sexual perversion always involves the actual use of the body.

By definition perversion embraces some specific and characteristic features which correspond to a dysfunction of the sexual component of personality development. In some cases perversions may be encapsulated from the rest of the personality so that on the surface the person appears totally normal (Hopper 1991). This is because perversion involves a deep split between genital sexuality as a living, or loving, force, and what appears to be genital sexuality, but is actually pregenital. The pregenitality of perversions poses some intriguing considerations about female sexuality that require further understanding. We are aware that women can obtain full sexual gratification almost ‘accidentally’ and unexpectedly from pregenital activities, for example, the caressing of the body, breast-feeding and even fantasizing.

Neither the International Classification of Disorders nor DSM III R (APA 1987) includes a definition of perversion based on a developmental perspective. For that matter, neither offers a clear and distinct explanation of the sexual outcome of perversion. This may derive from the fact that there are many individual sexual responses: the so-called ‘norms’ are characterized by very large standard deviations, which are even larger in women because they have a wider range of sexual responses. I would, therefore, propose that the necessary outcome for perversion in both sexes is sexual relief which brings about a transitory state of satisfaction from an increasing tension that is felt to be sexual tension.

The Holocaust and the Power of Powerlessness: Survivor Guilt an Unhealed Wound

Alfred Garwood

Alfred Garwood

The Old Hall Surgery, 237 Hall Lane, Chingford E4 8HX

Alfred Garwood  

The four elements of the trauma suffered by Holocaust survivors are powerlessness, annihilation anxiety, object loss and torture. A central and persistent component of the so-called survivor syndrome is survivor guilt. Classical theories of guilt do not explain it satisfactorily. Psychoanalysis or psychodynamic therapy for survivors is one of the most difficult challenges due to the powerful countertransferences that the therapists must struggle with. The essential psychic process underlying survivor guilt is self blame which is a defensive omnipotent phantasy. Powerlessness and annihilation threat resurrect unconscious memories of neonatal helplessness, dependency, vulnerability and primal agony, generating the need for defensive omnipotence. In the traumatic environment created by the Nazis, self blame was virtually the inevitable psychic defence. It has persisted because mourning is obstructed by the conscious and unconscious fear of being overwhelmed by the re-emergence of the originating feelings of powerlessness, annihilation anxiety and pain of object loss. Adaptive and maladaptive defences are used throughout later life which attempt to avoid powerlessness and loss. Healing can still take place through creative reparation and memorialization which may facilitate successful mourning.

I found this clinical material both very interesting and particularly relevant to understanding some of the difficulties encountered in the treatment of disturbed adolescents. Paul might be seen as representative of many adolescents who desperately need psychotherapeutic help. Despite obvious risks and difficulties, Paul's frequent missed sessions (mainly before breaks) and his rather provocative and threatening way of relating, this boy seemed to me to be capable of valuing and using his therapy.

Paul seems a very vulnerable adolescent who feels trapped in an impossible situation: he wants his therapist to know about his anxieties, to see how fragmented and mad he feels, to see his anxieties about his sexuality, to tackle his ‘fakedness’, to see how he cannot bear knowledge of his loving feelings without distorting them in a perverse way, while, at the same time, whenever his therapist does try to approach this, it is experienced as an attack. It seems to me that whenever he is confronted with his own psychic reality, he feels threatened and attacked by the therapist who is experienced as containing the projections of his own ‘madness’.

Pauline Dalal  

These two books form part of a series of five in which therapists representing different types of therapy are given the transcript of an introductory interview with a potential client. The therapists may address questions to the client through a mediator and then write what they think is happening, how they would proceed in therapy, and make some prediction as to the outcome. The final chapter presents the client's views of what they say.

The aim is to explore different approaches in an inclusive way and to consider how some may be better suited to certain presenting issues and personalities. The two volumes presented a wide range of therapies: psychoanalytic, cognitive analytic, transactional analysis, Gestalt, person-centred, humanistic-transpersonal, integrative, art therapy, cognitive behavioural, feminist, group and brief psychotherapy. In spite of this spectrum, they shared certain elements in common. Understandably, all stressed the importance of the live encounter in any therapy relationship, though some more than others emphasized their sense of limitation in its absence. All took up the importance of loss in the presenting material, as well as early experiences and relationships. All mention the role of the individual client in the process of change.

For some, the social and political context plays an important and, in certain cases, crucial role. Several include behavioural styles of facilitating, either extensively or as part of a broader kit. This means that some styles are much more directive than others. Also, a number of them readily accept the conscious expression and experience of the client, or emphasize environmental failure rather than the notion of inner conflict and of the unconscious, which are fundamental to the analytic schools.

In this way, the books do provoke thought about models of being human and models of therapy. The therapists' comments bring to mind philosophical and clinical questions: what is innate, what is the self, what is real, is the gender of the therapist significant or not, should the external world be included or excluded, does an unconscious exist, what is the goal of the therapy model, does the picture of the client appear to sacrifice the constructive, healthy aspects of the person or the obstructive and destructive elements? They underline the inevitable relativity of any theory.

Carol Topolski

Carol Topolski

London

Carol Topolski  

For a dozen years of my adulthood, and after having my own children, I worked as a film censor, refracting screen images through my own psychological prism in order to judge and understand their social meaning. As a consequence, my mind is littered - seared - with unbidden and unwanted images which lurch sometimes painfully from their hiding-places. One such imprint is a nasty little film called Mother's Day. In this, a cackling spider-mother sits in her nest in the middle of a woods-web from which she sends her two dumb sons out to rape, mutilate and torture passers-by. They bring back stories of their murderous exploits to excite her, sometimes bringing the victims, too, as thrilling live entertainment: sadism on stage. Wicked they are, evil she is, but she loves her sons. Compare this with the Virgin Mary, passive receptacle for Godseed, woman shriven of her own desire, portrayed ubiquitously as unalloyed love, the Madonna-and-child, infinite fidelity - and she loves her son, too. The one image a perversion of maternity, the other an ideal - and an ideal uncorrupted by maternal hatred. Rozsika Parker, in this provocative and enthralling book, treads carefully but resolutely down a path whose shape is frequently differently mapped from the shape she discovers as she explores maternal ambivalence. Methodically - but never pedantically - she addresses the discourse of the mentors of the twentieth-century psychoanalytic world, considering their view of what constitutes good-enough mothering and taking issue with those who would argue that maternal ambivalence is inevitably pathogenic. She points to the dynamic thrust of much psychoanalytic thinking whose focus is the child, from Winnicott's baby with her environmental mother, to Mahler's toddler taking her first teetering steps away as she separates and individuates.

Parker performs an enriching volte-face as she contemplates the phenomenon of the discomfiting coexistence of love and hate of her baby from the mother's point of view. She examines the mother's development from Winnicott's ‘object-relating’ to ‘use of an object’ maturity; the mother's negotiation of her move to Klein's depressive position and the mother's capacity for Bion's reverie about herself and her own needs, all of which grow to the sequence of moments when she can separate from her child as a healthy adult herself.

Phil Mollon

Phil Mollon

Stevenage, Herts SG1 4AB

Phil Mollon  

An emerging clarity about the trauma-based nature of many severe mental states was thrown into confusion by the realization in the early 1990s that some memories of childhood abuse might be ‘false memories’. However, the debate about memory often generates simplistic and unproductive arguments in an area which is inherently eomplex and confusing and pervaded by ambiguity. ‘Memories’ are often best regarded as psychodynamic products, not unlike dreams, mixing elements from various sourees. Motivated forgetting is not a mysterious process beyond the reaeh of introspection but is, in many instances, very ordinary and familiar. Patients who have suffered severely traumatizing childhoods often have very disturbed, or ‘mutilated’, states of consciousness; a narrative of abuse may be presented in one state of mind, with amnesia for this in another state of mind. Acknowledgement and tolerance of uncertainty form the appropriate stance for the therapist. Some guidelines are suggested for psychoanalytic therapists, designed to reduce the dangers of fostering, or colluding with, false memories of childhood abuse.

This paper considers Shakespeare's tragedy of Othello as a symbolic enactment of intrapsychic life. The developmental movement from the paranoid-schizoid to the depressive position and from narcissistic love, arising from the investment of parts of the self in another person, to real, interpersonal love, is arrested and finally ruined by the agency of a split-off lago element in the personality. Clinical Commentary XVIII

[The material was sent ‘blind’ to three clinicians who were asked to comment on the session and on how their way of thinking about the patient would inform their way of working with him. - MB]

The Therapist, a Woman, Writes

The patient, Paul, 16, has been in twice weekly psychotherapy for one year. He does not use the couch. He was referred by a hospital psychiatric department following assessment by a psychiatrist and child psychotherapist. He also underwent a medical investigation for severe headaches and high blood pressure both of which were thought to be linked to his emotional state.

Paul has been having problems since he was 9 years old. He was described as having very little internal control. He was often violent to himself and others, smashing his fist against walls, getting into fights, etc. He also damaged property, for instance, breaking up a class-room when 13, an event which led to his expulsion. He describes this expulsion as precipitating his ‘nervous breakdown’ when he came close to throwing himself from a railway bridge. He has continued to have episodes of depression and suicidal thoughts.

Since a young age Paul has turned to drugs (mainly cannabis) and alcohol in an attempt to obliterate pain. His consumption of both has decreased since therapy began but he still ‘binges’.

Paul is dyslexic and was attending a special school when he began therapy. He was on a very limited contract and hardly attended. He left aged only 15 without any qualifications. He worked full-time in a factory for a few months and was then unemployed. Though the work was exploitative it did provide him with a structure which helped hold him together.

Paul's father moved from Eastern Europe in the 1950s, worked his way through college to become an engineer and married Paul's mother. According to Paul this was their first relationship. She does voluntary work. Paul is the youngest of four children. There is a 10-year gap between him and the next sibling. There is a long history of psychiatric illness on his mother's side and his eldest sister is a manic-depressive now living in a special hostel. She was treated unsuccessfully at the same clinic when adolescent. Paul speaks fondly of his sister though is in touch with his anxiety, shared also by his parents, that he might ‘end up like her’. Paul seems very close to his mother whom he presents as concerned though indulgent, colluding with his acting-out. His father is portrayed as a tyrant whom Paul parodies with contempt.

David Mann  

In common with writers such as Chasseguet-Smirgel, McDougall and Meltzer, Sheldon Bach defines perversion not through activity but as a state of mind. Specifically it is ‘the treatment of another person as a thing rather than a human being that I see as a perversion of object relationships’, and this forms the basis of the book. Bach casts his net widely to include a variety of human phenomena in his discussion: ‘Perversion in this sense is a lack of capacity for whole-object love, and while this often includes sexual perversions, it also includes certain character perversions, character disorders, and psychotic conditions’ (pp. xv-xvi). The rest of the book goes on to explore this thesis from various directions including discussion of eating and narcissistic disorders.

The issue is one of how one person can degrade another to the status of a thing. ‘From a certain perspective, one might say that a person has a perversion instead of having a relationship’ (author's italics, p. 5). The author suggests that people with perversions cannot tolerate ambiguity. For example, the sadomasochist feels himself living in two worlds: a fantasy world of omnipotent idealization of self and object, and the real world which is too dangerous to live in. At root is a problem in relating to parents during infancy, such as a failure to integrate the mother of nurturance and pleasure with the mother of frustration and pain. An observation such as this brings Bach close to the Kleinian school, though he cites the work of Winnicott much more than Klein. Bach, in the tradition of Winnicott, goes on to suggest that the sadist is displaying a sort of temper tantrum, playing at destroying the object for pleasure. Since the object is not destroyed this gives perverse meaning: ‘I can do anything I want to you and you'll still always be there’ (p. 17).

What is the Difference between A ‘Psychoanalytic’ and A So-Called ‘Normal’, Everyday Relationship? The Controversy between Freud and Ferenczi

Carla Russell

Carla Russell

Carla Russell  

Is the form Freud gave to the analytic relationship definitive? This question will be answered by analysing the argumentation in the Freud-Ferenczi controversy concerning the design of the therapeutic relationship. The current albeit superficial mode of interpretation of this controversy is mainly in terms of a supposed ‘warm’ emotional involvement of the analyst, as opposed to his ‘cold’ aloofness. Fundamentally however, the controversy concerns the way one should delineate the psychoanalytic relationship, as a method of treatment, from our everyday relationships. Freud and Ferenczi are the historical figures exemplifying what can be considered an ongoing debate.

… My recommendations on technique given at the time were essentially negative. I considered it most important to underline what should not be done and to show the temptations opposing analysis. Almost everything to be done positively I left to the ‘tact’ introduced by you. But I aimed not at the obedients who were not aware of the elasticity of my remarks and subjected themselves to my recommendations as if they were taboo-regulations. This should be revised one day, without, however, doing away with the obligations.

Freud in a letter to Ferenczi, 4.1.1928 (Ferenczi 1928a, p. 99)

Clinical Commentary XIX

[The material was sent to the three commentators, asking them to take up areas that interested them about the content of the session or the technique of the therapist. - KA]

The patient is a lesbian woman who has been in therapy once weekly for three years. She had never had a sexual relationship with a man. The original reason for seeking psychotherapy had been periods of depression, particularly about work. The experience was of being under intense and unremitting pressure, such that there was very little scope to find enjoyment in life. She was in a relationship which had lasted a number of years and the couple were buying a house together. The two partners had very different experiences in their families of origin: one had an unusually close family - there were family gatherings most weeks to celebrate birthdays and anniversaries which were attended by 20 or 30 people from different parts of the country, while the other had a more scattered and fragmented family. Both families were welcoming to the other partner. Over the period of therapy the work situation had eased as we understood how claustrophobic the patient felt. At the same time other issues, such as future plans especially about children, had emerged tentatively, often to disappear again as work would again come to the fore. In the original discussion about starting therapy the question of coming twice weekly was raised, but was never taken up on the grounds of expense. It was at times very clear that this added to a sense of restriction in the therapy which, it seemed, had to be put up with for fear of disturbance elsewhere. The sessions tended to be full and interesting but often with the sense of limitation alluded to above.

The previous session had to be missed because of work commitments. As usual she had given warning and notice of the fact that this would happen.

The Session

When she arrived on time she took her shoes off, as was her custom, and put them neatly on the far side of my small consulting-room before lying down on the couch. Her first comment was to realize suddenly that she had not brought the cheque she had written out to pay the bill I had given her a fortnight ago. She apologized and said she would post it. I commented that perhaps the forgetting was related to the fact that we had to miss our last session. She told me that she had written the cheque on Friday when she had returned home, along with other bills that had accumulated over the week. It had been left on the table in the kitchen where it had got left with other papers. Her partner is maybe more prone to leave things there than she is herself.
