David Mann

David Mann

London

David Mann  

Traditionally women therapists have written much less than their male colleagues about the erotic transference and countertransference. In the last few years this trend has been corrected by the publication of several books by women writers about the erotic in psychoanalysis. This, by W rye and Welles, stands out impressively as a major contribution to our understanding.

The focus of the book is the erotic nature of pre-oedipal experience between mother and child and how this is replayed in the transference/countertransference. The authors acknowledge that working with this early erotic material is difficult but is a ‘goldmine’ if worked through in the analysis: ‘The greatest danger to analyst and patient alike is they may fail to recognize early eroticism’ (p. 86). The subject is explored in four sections: story-making, maternal erotic transferences and countertransferences, perversions as derangements of desire and, finally, permutations and transformations related to gender.

Classical object relations theory has tended to focus on the nurturing side of the mother while ignoring the erotic aspects. Wrye and Welles take up this neglect. They emphasize the sensual bonding or ‘body loveprinting’ (p. 34) between mother and baby. This forms the basis of all eroticism. The two authors locate the origins of erotic experience in the contacts dealing with body fluids: after the amniotic fluid comes milk, drool, urine, faeces, mucus, spit, tears, perspiration. The seminal and vaginal fluids of adult erotic play are a symbolic extension of the earliest sensual fluids. The mother's ministrations of these fluids create a sensual adhesion to the relationship. The maternal erotic transference and erotic countertransference recreate the sensual erotic contact between mother and infant; the maternal erotic transference is a positive and necessary transforming phenomenon in psychoanalytic treatments.

The maternal erotic transference may first manifest in the analytic setting in concrete fantasies about the real parts of the therapist's body. If the therapist can have access to his or her own maternal erotic countertransference, he or she makes possible the patient's acceptance of the maternal erotic transference, with its loving and sadomasochistic permutations - thus fostering a sense of wholeness.

Adolescent Phantasies and the Horror Film

Ivan Ward

Ivan Ward

20 Maresfield Gardens, London NW3 5SX

Ivan Ward  

The Freud Museum conference on Adolescent Phantasies and the Horror Film Genre took place at the National Film Theatre on 18 March 1995. The audience was composed largely of teachers, film theorists and cultural historians. There was apparently little interest in the topic among psychotherapists. Despite this, I believe the conference addressed a significant area of study, and I would like to offer the following comments to indicate why.

There is no doubt that the contemplation of horror is disturbing to many people. In the first place, horror stories frighten their audiences and produce a visceral reaction: thrills and excitement for adolescents, nausea and revulsion for most adults. Under these circumstances it is all too easy to confuse real horror with horror stories and fail to give due consideration to either psychic reality or narrative form. The techniques of horror stories exploit this propensity to the full.

A second reason for our disturbance may be that the existence of the horror genre upsets the distinction we are apt to maintain between the normal and the pathological. Clearly there is something ‘pathological’ about the avid consumption of horror, and yet it is quite normal in many cultures, including our own. For the purposes of the present remarks the distinction is not particularly relevant. The issue is whether the films can tell us something about adolescent psychology.

Psychotherapists, however, rarely deal with film material in their work. They are generally used to hearing about their patient's phantasies rather than seeing them portrayed, and the visual impact of film is in many ways quite alien to the culture of psychoanalysis. Although his ideas were changed to some extent by the work of Melanie Klein, it is true to say that Freud's legacy of dealing with phantasies as either a structure (as in primal phantasies) or a narrative (as in day-dreams) missed out the bodily effects and experiences which often accompany them. For instance, a young man may be walking along the road and suddenly imagine that a dog he sees walking towards him has bitten off his hand. He experiences a rush of adrenalin and pulls his hand away involuntarily. Or he may catch the eye of a stranger across the street and imagine he is an assailant with a knife in his hand and the intention to disembowel him. A shiver goes down his back, and once again the phantasy engenders a real experience with bodily effects. No doubt these conscious phantasies are related to deep unconscious ones which may have a quite different emotional tone. The content of a horror-phantasy can also be experienced without any overt sensations of terror.
